FACTION_DESC_WESSEX: King Beorhtric has married Offa's daughter, making Wessex an ally of Mercia – but at the Frankish court lives the exiled Egbert, who will one day return. Rich southern lands, seated at Winchester.
FACTION_DESC_MERCIA: Offa, “king of the English”, is the greatest ruler of the age: London is his, Kent, Sussex and Essex are his vassals, and his dyke seals off Wales. But should he die, his empire may falter.
FACTION_DESC_NORTHUMBRIA: A land of scholars and saints – Lindisfarne, Jarrow, York – but torn by murderous dynastic strife: in 790 Æthelred I returned. In 793 the Vikings strike here for the first time.
FACTION_DESC_VIKINGS: In 790 the Danes still live overseas: they begin raiding from 835, and in 865 the Great Heathen Army arrives and captures York. They cannot be chosen at the start – the computer takes them over as soon as they gain land.
LOCKED_DESC: No diplomacy is possible with this land; it cannot be conquered or crossed.
LOCKED_NOTE: Strathclyde, Brittany and the Frankish Empire are locked: no diplomacy with them.

HIST_871: The "year of battles": Ashdown, Basing and Meretun. After King Æthelred dies, his brother Alfred takes the throne of Wessex.
HIST_872: The Great Heathen Army winters in London; the Mercians pay the Danes tribute.
HIST_873: The Danish army winters at Torksey in Lindsey.
HIST_874: At Repton the Danes drive out King Burgred of Mercia, who flees to Rome; Ceolwulf II is set in his place.
HIST_875: Halfdan marches into Northumbria, Guthrum to Cambridge. Alfred fights seven Danish ships at sea.
HIST_876: Halfdan shares out the lands of Northumbria among his men; Guthrum's army slips into Wareham.
HIST_877: The Danes move to Exeter; a storm off Swanage wrecks 120 of their ships. Mercia is partitioned.
HIST_878: After Twelfth Night Guthrum surprises Chippenham; Alfred flees to the marshes of Athelney, then wins at Edington in spring. Guthrum is baptised.
HIST_879: Guthrum's army moves from Chippenham to Cirencester.
HIST_880: Guthrum's army settles in East Anglia and shares out the land.
HIST_882: Alfred's fleet fights the crews of four Danish ships and captures two.
HIST_885: Alfred relieves the siege of Rochester; his fleet defeats sixteen Danish ships at the mouth of the Stour.
HIST_886: Alfred occupies London and entrusts it to Æthelred of Mercia; all the English not under Danish rule submit to him.
HIST_890: Guthrum, Danish king of East Anglia, dies.
HIST_892: A new Danish army comes from Francia: 250 ships land in Kent at Appledore.
HIST_893: Battles at Farnham and Buttington; the Danes besiege Exeter.
HIST_894: The Danes shelter within the deserted Roman walls of Chester.
HIST_895: The Danes build a fort on the River Lea above London.
HIST_896: Alfred has new warships built, larger than the Danes'; the Danish army disperses.
HIST_899: Alfred the Great dies on 26 October; his son Edward the Elder succeeds him.
HIST_900: Æthelwold, Alfred's nephew, rebels and flees to the Northumbrian Danes, who accept him as king.
HIST_902: Battle of the Holme: Æthelwold and Eohric, Danish king of East Anglia, are killed.
HIST_907: Æthelflæd has the walls of Chester rebuilt.
HIST_909: Edward's army ravages Northumbria; the relics of St Oswald are brought to Gloucester.
HIST_910: At Tettenhall the English defeat the Northumbrian Danes.
HIST_911: Æthelred, Lord of the Mercians, dies; his widow Æthelflæd rules. Edward takes London and Oxford.
HIST_913: Æthelflæd builds burhs at Tamworth and Stafford.
HIST_917: Æthelflæd captures Derby; Edward brings East Anglia to submission.
HIST_918: Æthelflæd enters Leicester and York offers her allegiance; she dies at Tamworth in June.
HIST_919: Ragnall seizes York; Edward takes direct rule of Mercia.
HIST_920: At Bakewell the northern lords all acknowledge Edward as overlord.
HIST_924: Edward the Elder dies; his son Æthelstan becomes king.
HIST_927: Æthelstan takes York: the first king of all the English people.
HIST_934: Æthelstan leads a campaign into Scotland.
HIST_937: Battle of Brunanburh: Æthelstan defeats the alliance of the Scots, Strathclyde and the Dublin Vikings.
HIST_939: Æthelstan dies; Edmund I succeeds. Olaf Guthfrithson seizes York.
HIST_942: Edmund recovers the Five Boroughs: Derby, Leicester, Lincoln, Nottingham and Stamford.
HIST_944: Edmund drives the Norse kings out of York.
HIST_946: Edmund I is murdered at Pucklechurch; his brother Eadred takes the throne.
HIST_948: Eadred burns Ripon; York takes in Eric Bloodaxe.
HIST_954: Eric Bloodaxe falls at Stainmore: Northumbria becomes part of England for good.
HIST_959: On Eadwig's death Edgar becomes king of all England.

HIST_973: Edgar is crowned at Bath; at Chester six kings row him on the Dee in token of submission.
HIST_978: King Edward the Martyr is murdered at Corfe; his brother Æthelred takes the throne.
HIST_991: Battle of Maldon: Ealdorman Byrhtnoth falls against the Vikings; for the first time England pays tribute (gafol) – 10,000 pounds.
HIST_1002: On St Brice's Day, at Æthelred's order, the Danes living in England are massacred.
HIST_1013: Sweyn Forkbeard conquers England; Æthelred flees to Normandy.
HIST_1016: Battle of Assandun: Cnut defeats Edmund Ironside and after Edmund's death becomes king of all England.
HIST_1042: Edward the Confessor becomes King of England.
HIST_1065: The Northumbrians rise against Earl Tostig; Westminster Abbey is consecrated.
HIST_1066: Edward the Confessor dies; Harold defeats Harald Hardrada at Stamford Bridge, then falls at Hastings against William's army.
HIST_1086: William the Conqueror has the great survey of the realm made: the Domesday Book.

EVENT_GOSPEL_BOOK_DESC: The monks of {0} would make a gilded gospel book if the king pays for the vellum and pigments.
EVENT_SPY_DESC: We have caught an enemy spy disguised as a travelling merchant.
EVENT_WEDDING_OFFER_DESC: An envoy has come from the court of {0}: {1} would gladly give a kinswoman in marriage to our royal house.
EVENT_WAREHAM_OATH_DESC: The Danish army has withdrawn into Wareham and, swearing on their holy ring, offers peace and hostages. Can we trust their oath?
EVENT_WAREHAM_OATH_C2: Do not trust them – stay under arms
EVENT_ATHELNEY_DESC: After Twelfth Night Guthrum fell upon Chippenham. The king fled with a handful of followers into the marshes of Athelney. What shall we do?
EVENT_ATHELNEY_C1: Hide and gather the army in secret
EVENT_EDINGTON_DESC: After seven weeks in hiding, the men of Somerset, Wiltshire and Hampshire gather around their king at Egbert's Stone. The time for Edington has come.
EVENT_EDMUND_MARTYR_DESC: King Edmund, slain by the Danes in 869, is revered by the people as a saint, and miracles are told at his tomb.
EVENT_GUTHRUM_BAPTISM_DESC: The English demand that Guthrum be baptised at Aller, taking the Christian name Æthelstan.
EVENT_LONDON_RESTORED_DESC: The trading town of Lundenwic is deserted. Within the old Roman walls a new town could rise, as Alfred did in 886.
EVENT_LONDON_RESTORED_C2: Entrust the town to an ealdorman
EVENT_BURGHAL_HIDAGE_DESC: By the Burghal Hidage, every pole of wall needs four men. Shall we build a network of forts so that no one lives more than a day's march from a burh?
EVENT_AETHELFLAED_BURHS_DESC: Æthelflæd, Lady of the Mercians, is raising burhs from Bridgnorth to Warwick. Shall we follow her example?
EVENT_BRUNANBURH_DESC: Olaf of Dublin, Constantine of the Scots and the Britons of Strathclyde have invaded with a great host. Æthelstan summons every Englishman to battle.
EVENT_MALDON_GAFOL_DESC: Ealdorman Byrhtnoth has fallen at Maldon. Archbishop Sigeric advises paying the Danes a gafol of 10,000 pounds.
EVENT_ST_BRICE_DESC: King Æthelred has ordered that all Danes living in England be slain on 13 November. Shall we carry out the order?
EVENT_SWEYN_REVENGE_DESC: Gunnhild, sister of King Sweyn of Denmark, died in the massacre. Sweyn has sworn revenge, and his ships are bound for {0}.
EVENT_ASSANDUN_DESC: The armies of Edmund Ironside and Cnut face each other at Assandun. Eadric Streona's loyalty wavers.

EVENT_COURT_DESC: The king has summoned the Witan at Easter. Decide the policy for the year ahead!

FACTION_DESC_KENT: With the archbishop's seat at Canterbury, Kent is the oldest Christian English kingdom, but since 785 Offa has ruled it directly. A single, rich province – if Offa dies, you can throw off the yoke.
FACTION_DESC_ESSEX: The kingdom of the East Saxons around Colchester. London was lost to the Mercians long ago; King Sigeric is Offa's vassal. Small, but stands at the gateway of the Thames.
FACTION_DESC_SUSSEX: The land of the South Saxons between the Weald and the sea, with the bishopric of Selsey. Offa subdued it in 771; its ealdormen rule it. Small, but easily defended.
FACTION_DESC_SCOTS: The Gaelic kingdom of Dál Riata between the mountains of Argyll and the Hebrides, with the fortress rock of Dunadd and Saint Columba's Iona. A seafaring people, defending harder in the Highlands. In 843 Cináed mac Ailpín unites the Scots and the Picts.
FACTION_DESC_PICTS: The “painted people”, the kingdom of Fortriu from the Tay to Caithness. Caustantín mac Fergusa is a mighty king, but from the north the Norwegians threaten. They defend harder in the Highlands.
FACTION_DESC_IRISH: Ireland's dozen kingdoms gather around the High King of Tara, Donnchad Midi. Saint Patrick's Armagh and the great monasteries are rich – which is why, from 795, the Vikings come too.
HIST_790: In Northumbria Osred II is deposed and tonsured a monk; the exiled Æthelred I returns. Offa, “king of the English”, is at the height of his power.
HIST_792: Offa's Kentish charter is the first to mention defence against “pagan seamen”. King Æthelred of Northumbria marries Offa's daughter, Ælfflæd.
HIST_793: Terrible omens over Northumbria: whirlwinds, lightning and fiery dragons in the sky, followed by great famine. On 8 June the heathens ravage God's church on the island of Lindisfarne – the Viking Age begins.
HIST_794: Offa has King Æthelberht of East Anglia beheaded. The Vikings plunder Jarrow, Bede's monastery, but their ships are wrecked in a storm.
HIST_795: The first Viking raids in Ireland and the Hebrides: the monasteries of Rechru (Rathlin) and Iona are ravaged.
HIST_796: Offa dies; his son Ecgfrith follows him to the grave 141 days later, and Coenwulf becomes king of Mercia. In Kent Eadberht Præn rebels, and in Northumbria King Æthelred is murdered.
HIST_798: Coenwulf crushes the Kentish revolt, has Eadberht Præn blinded, and sets his brother Cuthred over Kent.
HIST_802: Beorhtric dies (tradition says his wife Eadburh poisoned him); Egbert, returning from Frankish exile, becomes king of Wessex. At Kempsford the men of Wiltshire defeat the Hwicce. The Vikings burn Iona.
HIST_806: The Vikings kill sixty-eight monks on Iona; Saint Columba's community withdraws to Kells in Ireland. In Northumbria King Eardwulf is driven out.
HIST_811: Caustantín, king of the Picts, also gains Dál Riata: the two peoples grow ever more intertwined.
HIST_815: Egbert ravages Cornwall from east to west.
HIST_825: The Battle of Ellendun: Egbert defeats Beornwulf, king of Mercia. Kent, Surrey, Sussex and Essex submit to Wessex; the East Angles kill Beornwulf.
HIST_829: Egbert conquers Mercia, and at Dore Northumbria submits too: the chronicle names him the eighth bretwalda, lord of Britain.
HIST_830: Wiglaf recovers the throne of Mercia. Egbert marches against Wales and forces its submission.
HIST_835: Heathen men ravage the Isle of Sheppey: the Danes have arrived.
HIST_836: Egbert clashes at Carhampton with the crews of thirty-five ships; the Danes are victorious.
HIST_838: At Hingston Down Egbert defeats the alliance of the Cornish and the Danes.
HIST_839: Egbert dies; his son Æthelwulf becomes king of Wessex. The Vikings shatter the Picts: King Eóganán falls, along with his brother Bran and the flower of the nobility.
HIST_841: The Norwegians raise a longphort, a fortified ship-camp, at the mouth of the Liffey: Dublin is born.
HIST_842: Great slaughter in London and Rochester: the Vikings strike the trading towns too.
HIST_843: Cináed mac Ailpín, king of the Scots, also gains the throne of the Picts: Alba, the kingdom of Scotland, is being born.
HIST_845: Ragnar's Vikings besiege Paris at Easter; Charles the Bald buys peace with 7,000 pounds of silver.
HIST_850: For the first time the heathens winter on English soil, on the Isle of Thanet.
HIST_851: 350 ships land at the Thames and sack Canterbury and London; Æthelwulf wins a great victory at Aclea.
HIST_853: Wessex and Mercia march together against Wales; Æthelwulf gives his daughter in marriage to King Burgred of Mercia. Young Alfred is sent to Rome.
HIST_858: Æthelwulf dies; his son Æthelbald becomes king of Wessex, and marries his father's widow, Judith.
HIST_860: A Danish army storms Winchester, but the men of Hampshire and Berkshire put them to flight.
HIST_865: The Great Heathen Army lands in East Anglia under Ívarr and Ubba. The East Angles give them horses for peace.
HIST_866: On All Saints' Day the Great Army takes York; Northumbria is divided by the dynastic strife of Osberht and Ælla.
HIST_867: Osberht and Ælla besiege York together, and both fall; the Danes set a puppet king on Northumbria's throne.
HIST_869: The Great Army kills King Edmund of East Anglia, who refuses to renounce his faith.
HIST_870: The Danes make camp at Reading, and turn against Wessex.

MISSION_UNITE_ENGLAND_DESC: Unite the English under the banner of Wessex: be lord of all fifteen English provinces, from Exeter to Bamburgh.
MISSION_OFFA_EMPIRE_DESC: Make Mercia lord of all southern England: let every English land south of the Humber be yours.
MISSION_NORTHERN_CROWN_DESC: Restore Northumbria's golden age: rule from the Humber to the Forth, together with Lindsey, Fortriu and Dál Riata.
MISSION_WUFFINGA_DESC: Raise East Anglia to the splendour of King Rædwald's age: let Essex, London, Kent and Lindsey also be yours.
MISSION_KENT_FREE_DESC: Throw off Mercia's yoke, and make Kent once more lord of southern England, as in the days of King Æthelberht.
MISSION_ESSEX_LONDON_DESC: Win London back from the Mercians, and make Essex lord of the Thames region.
MISSION_SUSSEX_SOUTH_DESC: King Ælle's people rise again: be lord of the southern coast from Winchester to Canterbury, together with London.
MISSION_ARMES_PRYDEIN: Armes Prydein – The Prophecy of Britain
MISSION_ARMES_PRYDEIN_DESC: Win back the land of the ancient Britons: Wales, Man, Dumnonia (Exeter), the Old North (Carlisle, Whithorn) and the heart of Mercia.
MISSION_KINGDOM_OF_ALBA_DESC: Unite the Scots and the Picts: let Dál Riata, Pictland and Lothian be yours.
MISSION_PICTISH_REALM_DESC: Make Fortriu a realm ruling from sea to sea: Pictland, Dál Riata, Orkney and Lothian.
MISSION_HIGH_KING_DESC: Be the undisputed High King of all Ireland: Tara, Ulster, Munster, Connacht, Leinster and Man.
MISSION_KINGDOM_OF_ISLES_DESC: Forge a sea-kingdom: Orkney, the Hebrides, Argyll, Man, Dublin and Galloway.
MISSION_CONQUEST_ENGLAND_DESC: Cross the Channel, and seize the heart of England: Canterbury, Chichester, Winchester, London and York.
MISSION_DANELAW_DESC: Make York, the Midlands and East Anglia into the land of Danish law.
ACH_LINDISFARNE_DESC: Defend the monastery of Lindisfarne against the heathens in 793.
ACH_IONA_DESC: Defend the monastery of Iona against the Vikings.
ACH_BRETWALDA_DESC: Be lord of all fifteen English provinces.
ACH_SMALL_KINGDOM_DESC: As Kent, Essex or Sussex, rule four provinces.
ACH_BURHS_DESC: Have five fortified sites (burh, dún, dinas…).
ACH_ALLIANCE_DESC: Make a marriage alliance with another kingdom.
ACH_INDEPENDENCE_DESC: As Kent, Essex or Sussex, throw off Mercia's yoke.
ACH_YEAR_871_DESC: Reach 871, the year Alfred the Great took the throne.
ACH_YEAR_1066_DESC: Reach the year of the Battle of Hastings.
EVENT_OFFA_DYKE_M_DESC: King Offa would raise a mighty earthwork against the Welsh, from the mouth of the Dee to the Severn. The work will need thousands of hands.
EVENT_FIRST_VOYAGE_DESC: The sea-kings hear word that in the west, on Christian shores, rich and undefended monasteries stand. Shall we build ships, or live by trade?
EVENT_LINDISFARNE_AFTERMATH_DESC: From Charlemagne's court, Alcuin, the scholar of York, writes a letter to King Æthelred: “Never before has such terror struck Britain… the church of Saint Cuthbert has become the prey of the heathens.” He urges penance – others press for the guarding of the coasts.
EVENT_LINDISFARNE_AFTERMATH_C2: We post watch on the coasts
EVENT_AETHELBERHT_VISIT_DESC: King Offa has invited King Æthelberht to Sutton Walls, to marry his daughter Ælfthryth. His counsellors fear a trap.
EVENT_AETHELBERHT_VISIT_C2: We do not go – we prepare for war
EVENT_EADBERHT_PRAEN_DESC: Offa is dead! Eadberht Præn, the exiled priest, has returned from the Frankish court, proclaims himself King of Kent, and calls the men of Kent to rebellion against Mercia.
EVENT_RHUDDLAN_DESC: After Offa's death the Mercians gather at Rhuddlan against the Welsh. Shall we meet them on the marshy plain?
EVENT_CHARLEMAGNE_COAST_DESC: Charlemagne himself inspects the fortifications of the Channel coast, and orders a fleet against the northmen.
EVENT_CHARLEMAGNE_COAST_C2: We trust in God and the Emperor
EVENT_EGBERT_RETURNS_DESC: Beorhtric has died; Egbert, son of Ealhmund, once driven out by Offa and Beorhtric, returns home from Frankish exile. The men of Wiltshire already stand at the border facing the Hwicce.
EVENT_IONA_RELICS_DESC: The Vikings have killed sixty-eight monks on Iona. The abbot asks that we bring Saint Columba's relics to safety, and build them a new church.
EVENT_IONA_RELICS_C1: A new church for the relics
EVENT_ELLENDUN_DESC: King Beornwulf of Mercia marches against Wessex. Egbert awaits him at Ellendun, near Wroughton.
EVENT_SUBMIT_TO_EGBERT_DESC: Egbert's son Æthelwulf arrives with a great army, and demands that we acknowledge the King of Wessex as our lord.
EVENT_EOGANAN_FALL_DESC: The Vikings have shattered our army: King Eóganán, his brother Bran, and the flower of the nobility have fallen. Where shall a new army come from?
EVENT_EOGANAN_FALL_C2: We seek peace with the Scots
EVENT_DUBLIN_LONGPHORT_DESC: Norwegian ships have wintered at the mouth of the Liffey, and are building a fortified camp, a longphort. Shall we fall upon them, or trade with them?
EVENT_CINAED_DESC: The royal house of the Picts has weakened under the blows of the Vikings. Cináed mac Ailpín, king of the Scots, lays claim through his mother's line to the throne of the Picts.

EVENT_CINAED_C2: We make peace with the Picts

RULER_ALFRED_BIO:
King of Wessex 871–899, the only English king called “the Great”.
In 878 he beat Guthrum's great Danish army at Edington.
Fortified towns (burhs), a fleet and a rotating levy kept the peace.
He issued a law code and had Latin works turned into English.
RULER_EDWARD_BIO:
Alfred's son, King of Wessex 899–924, who won back the Danelaw.
With his sister Æthelflæd he pushed north, building burh after burh.
By 918 East Anglia and the Five Boroughs had submitted to him.
At his death all English land south of the Humber obeyed one king.
RULER_AETHELSTAN_BIO:
Son of Edward the Elder; king of the English from 924, of “all Britain” from 927.
In 927 he took York — the first man to rule the whole of England.
At Brunanburh in 937 he crushed a Scots-Dublin-Strathclyde alliance.
His court had European fame; his sisters married Frankish and German princes.
RULER_EDMUND_BIO:
Æthelstan's brother, king of the English 939–946, crowned at barely eighteen.
He first lost, then by 944 won back the Five Boroughs and York.
He handed Strathclyde to the King of Scots in return for an alliance.
At a feast in Pucklechurch an outlawed robber stabbed him to death.
RULER_EADRED_BIO:
Brother of Edmund I, king of the English 946–955, sickly all his life.
Twice he drove the Norse kings out of York.
With Eric Bloodaxe's fall in 954 York became English for good.
He favoured Abbot Dunstan, later Archbishop of Canterbury.
RULER_EADWIG_BIO:
Son of Edmund I, king of the English 955–959, crowned at fifteen.
He walked out of his own coronation feast; Dunstan fetched him back and made an enemy.
In 957 Mercia and Northumbria chose his brother Edgar instead.
He died at barely twenty, and the realm was reunited under Edgar.
RULER_EDGAR_BIO:
King of the English 959–975; not one Viking raid struck the island in his reign.
With Dunstan he reformed and refounded the Benedictine houses.
He unified the coinage: every coin was recalled and restruck every few years.
Crowned at Bath in 973, he was then rowed on the Dee by British kings.
RULER_BURGRED_BIO:
King of Mercia 852–874, ally and brother-in-law of Wessex.
With Æthelwulf he broke the power of Rhodri in Wales.
At Nottingham in 868 he bought peace from the great Danish army.
Driven out in 874, he went as a pilgrim to Rome and died there.
RULER_CEOLWULF_BIO:
The last king of Mercia, 874–879, ruling by Danish favour.
The Chronicle mocks him as a “foolish king's thegn”, yet he struck his own coin.
A joint coinage with Alfred shows he was no simple puppet.
In 877 the Danes partitioned Mercia and kept its eastern half.
RULER_AETHELRED_M_BIO:
Lord of the Mercians 883–911; he took no royal title and acknowledged Alfred.
He married Alfred's daughter Æthelflæd.
In 886 Alfred gave London into his keeping, and he rebuilt its walls.
Even in sickness he led the Mercians beside his wife against the Danes.
RULER_AETHELFLAED_BIO:
Alfred's daughter, Lady of the Mercians 911–918, ruling alone after her husband's death.
She raised ten fortified towns from Chester to Warwick.
In 917 she took Derby, and in 918 Leicester surrendered to her.
Before she died even York offered to submit — such was her standing.
RULER_AELFWYNN_BIO:
Æthelflæd's daughter, Lady of the Mercians in 918 for only a few months.
She is the one woman in Mercia to inherit power from her mother.
Her uncle Edward the Elder deprived her of it that same year.
Taken into Wessex, she vanishes from the chronicles for good.
RULER_UNDER_WESSEX_BIO:
This land has no king of its own at this time.
The ruler of Wessex governs it through ealdormen and earls.
Its taxes and its levies serve the West Saxon king.
The old royal house has died out or lives on in submission.
RULER_EGBERT_I_BIO:
King of Northumbria 867–872 by Danish favour, after the fall of York.
He was obeyed south of the Tyne; in the north Bamburgh ruled itself.
In 872 the Northumbrians rose against him and drove him out.
He fled into Mercia and died in exile the following year.
RULER_RICSIGE_BIO:
King of Northumbria 873–876, after Egbert was driven out.
The Danes had not yet settled: each year they came back for tribute.
In 875 Halfdan's army wintered on the Tyne and harried the land.
With his death the kingdom of York passed to the Danes for good.
RULER_EGBERT_II_BIO:
King of what English Northumbria was left north of the Tyne, 876–878.
York and the lands south of it were already in Danish hands.
His title rested on the memory of the old house more than on real power.
After him the lords of Bamburgh styled themselves only earls.
RULER_EADWULF_BIO:
Lord of Bamburgh 878–913, head of what English Northumbria remained.
A northern source calls him a friend of King Alfred.
He kept his land by balancing between Danish York and the Scots.
At his death his son Ealdred inherited the rule north of the Tyne.
RULER_EALDRED_BIO:
Lord of Bamburgh 913–934, son of Eadwulf.
Driven out by the Norse Ragnall, he sought help from Edward the Elder.
Twice he fought the Norsemen of York at Corbridge.
At Eamont in 927 he accepted Æthelstan as his lord.
RULER_OSULF_BIO:
Lord of Bamburgh, and from 954 the first earl of all Northumbria.
He had a hand — not a clean one — in the fall of Eric Bloodaxe.
King Eadred entrusted him with both York and the Bamburgh lands.
Under him the old kingdom became a single English earldom.
RULER_EA_COIN_KINGS_BIO:
Under East Anglia's Danish lords, kings with English names struck coin.
The names Æthelred and Oswald survive only on those coins.
No chronicle writes a line of them; they were most likely puppets.
Yet their money shows that the form of the old order was kept up.
RULER_GUTHRUM_BIO:
A leader of the great Danish army, King of East Anglia 880–890.
In 878 Alfred defeated him at Edington.
He was baptised with Alfred as his godfather and took the name Æthelstan.
After the peace he settled down and struck coin under his Christian name.
RULER_EOHRIC_BIO:
Danish king of East Anglia after 890, Guthrum's successor.
He took in the pretender Æthelwold, cousin of Edward the Elder.
He fell in 902 at the battle of the Holme.
With his death the Danish kingdom of East Anglia lost its shine.
RULER_DANISH_JARLS_BIO:
Years without a king: the land was shared out among Danish jarls.
Each had his own following and levied his own dues.
They acted together only when common plunder or danger called.
That division made the West Saxon advance far easier.
RULER_HALFDAN_BIO:
A leader of the great Danish army, in tradition a son of Ragnar.
In 876 he shared out the land of Northumbria among his men.
So the Danes turned ploughmen, and the Danish kingdom of York was born.
He fell in 877 in Ireland, at Strangford Lough.
RULER_UNKNOWN_DANES_BIO:
Years from which not one Danish leader's name survives.
The chronicles speak only of “the host” and name no lord.
Power lay in several hands and changed owner fast.
The coins sometimes keep names that nothing else records.
RULER_GUTHRED_BIO:
Danish king of York from about 883; tradition says he was bought out of slavery to be made king.
The community of St Cuthbert raised him to the throne.
In his time Dane and Englishman lived side by side in peace.
He died in 895 and was buried in York Minster.
RULER_SIEFRED_BIO:
King of York in the 890s, after Guthred.
He is known almost only from his coins, kept alive by the moneyers.
His coins bear a Christian legend: Danish York had become a church town.
Some identify him with the Sigfred who raided on the Seine.
RULER_CNUT_BIO:
Danish king of York in the early 900s, perhaps ruling beside Siefred.
His name survives on thousands of coins; the chronicles barely mention him.
His money reads “Cnut rex” beside a cross.
He disappears in the early 900s, before the Norsemen came.
RULER_RAGNALL_BIO:
A Norse leader out of Dublin, King of York 918–921.
Twice he beat the Northumbrian English at Corbridge.
He was the first to join the Irish Sea and York under one hand.
In 920 he accepted Edward the Elder as his lord, then died.
RULER_SIHTRIC_BIO:
Kinsman of Ragnall, King of Dublin and then of York 921–927.
In 926 he married Æthelstan's sister at Tamworth.
He died a year later, and the marriage brought no peace.
His death gave Æthelstan the pretext to seize York.
RULER_OLAF_G_BIO:
King of Dublin and from 939 of York as well; son of Guthfrith.
In 937 he led the alliance against Æthelstan at Brunanburh.
Beaten there, he returned and took York anyway when Æthelstan died.
He died in 941 while campaigning against Bernicia.
RULER_OLAF_S_BIO:
Son of Sihtric, twice King of York (941–944 and 948–952).
As Amlaíb Cuarán he also ruled in Dublin.
He was baptised twice and twice driven out of York.
After fifty years of rule he died a monk on Iona.
RULER_ERIC_BIO:
Son of Harald Fairhair, King of Norway and then the last king of York.
The name “Bloodaxe” came from his fighting against his own brothers.
He ruled at York in 947–948 and again in 952–954.
Betrayed and killed at Stainmore in 954, he ended the kingdom of York.
RULER_EDWARD_MARTYR_BIO:
Son of Edgar the Peaceful, king of the English 975–978, still a boy.
In his reign the nobles quarrelled over the monasteries' lands.
In 978 he was murdered at the gate of Corfe, still in the saddle.
He was soon venerated as a saint: the martyr outgrew the living king.
RULER_AETHELRED_UNREADY_BIO:
King of the English 978–1013 and 1014–1016; the longest and most luckless reign.
His byname means “ill-counselled”, a pun on his own name.
Year after year he paid danegeld to the Viking armies.
In 1002 he ordered the St Brice's Day massacre, which brought a war of revenge.
RULER_SWEYN_BIO:
Son of Harald Bluetooth, King of Denmark from 986 and of England in 1013.
He won his throne by rising against his own father.
For years he taxed England, then campaigned there a whole year through.
All England submitted in 1013, but five weeks later he was dead.
RULER_CNUT_GREAT_BIO:
Son of Sweyn; King of England (1016), Denmark (1018) and Norway (1028).
He won at Assandun and took the whole realm when Edmund died.
He married Æthelred's widow Emma and ruled by English law.
His North Sea empire rose with him — and fell apart with him.
RULER_HAROLD_HAREFOOT_BIO:
Son of Cnut, King of England 1035–1040, at first only as regent.
His byname came from his swiftness, not from his battles.
He had a hand in the blinding and death of his half-brother Alfred.
He died before Harthacnut arrived; his body was later thrown into the Thames.
RULER_HARTHACNUT_BIO:
Son of Cnut and Emma, King of Denmark (1035) and England (1040).
He laid a heavy fleet-tax that provoked a rising at Worcester.
He had his half-brother's body dug up and dishonoured.
In 1042 he collapsed at a feast, drink in hand; the Danish line died with him.
RULER_EDWARD_CONFESSOR_BIO:
Son of Æthelred and Emma, King of England 1042–1066; half his life was spent in Normandy.
His reign was shaped by the struggle with the house of Godwin.
He built Westminster Abbey and died barely a week after its consecration.
He left no heir — and out of that came the three campaigns of 1066.
RULER_HAROLD_II_BIO:
Son of Godwin, Earl of Wessex, and the last Anglo-Saxon king of England, in 1066.
Crowned in January, he reigned barely nine months.
In September he destroyed Harald Hardrada at Stamford Bridge.
Three weeks later he fell at Hastings, facing William.
RULER_WILLIAM_CONQUEROR_BIO:
Duke of Normandy from 1035 and King of England from 1066, born out of wedlock.
He beat Harold at Hastings and was crowned at Westminster on Christmas Day.
He starved the rebel north into submission — the Harrying of the North.
At his order Domesday Book counted the wealth of all England.
RULER_WILLIAM_RUFUS_BIO:
Second son of the Conqueror, King of England 1087–1100.
His byname came from his ruddy face; the Church disliked him.
He fought both his brother Robert and his barons for power.
In 1100 an arrow killed him while hunting in the New Forest.
RULER_HENRY_I_BIO:
Youngest son of the Conqueror, King of England 1100–1135.
Within three days of his brother's death he had the treasury and the crown.
At Tinchebray in 1106 he beat Robert and won Normandy too.
He opened his reign with a charter of liberties, a forerunner of Magna Carta.
RULER_AELFHERE_BIO:
Ealdorman of Mercia 956–983, the mightiest magnate of Edgar's and Edward's day.
After Edgar died he led the seizing back of monastic lands.
His rival was Æthelwine, ealdorman of East Anglia.
It was he who had Edward the Martyr's body borne in state to Shaftesbury.
RULER_EADRIC_BIO:
Ealdorman of Mercia 1007–1017, the most notorious traitor of the age.
His byname means “the grasper”.
He changed sides between Æthelred and the Danes again and again, and fled at Assandun.
Cnut had him killed in the end: a man who betrayed all was wanted by none.
RULER_LEOFRIC_BIO:
Earl of Mercia 1026–1057, one of the great earls under Cnut and Edward.
He was the counterweight to the house of Godwin in the king's council.
With his wife Godgifu (Lady Godiva) he founded monasteries.
In 1051 it was his level head that kept England out of civil war.
RULER_AELFGAR_BIO:
Son of Leofric, Earl of East Anglia and later of Mercia.
Twice outlawed, twice he came back by force of arms.
He allied with Gruffydd of Wales and gave him his daughter.
His death opened the road to the throne for the house of Godwin.
RULER_EDWIN_BIO:
Son of Ælfgar, Earl of Mercia from 1062, and brother of Morcar.
Beaten at Fulford in 1066, he never reached Hastings.
He first submitted to William and then rebelled against him.
In 1071 his own men killed him as he fled.
RULER_UNDER_NORMANS_BIO:
After the Conquest this land has no ruler of its own.
The Norman king has parcelled it out among Norman barons.
The old English earls have fallen or gone into exile.
Castle and knight are the new signs of power in the countryside.
RULER_OSLAC_BIO:
Earl of York 966–975, a trusted man of King Edgar.
He kept order between Danish York and the English crown.
After Edgar's death, in 975, he was driven from the land.
The Chronicle laments him in verse as “the grey-haired hero”.
RULER_THORED_BIO:
Earl of York from about 979; his name betrays Danish descent.
His daughter Ælfgifu became the first wife of Æthelred II.
So he was the grandfather of Edmund Ironside.
He vanishes from the sources after a failed naval campaign in 992.
RULER_AELFHELM_BIO:
Earl of York 993–1006, in the reign of Æthelred.
His daughter Ælfgifu later became Cnut's English wife.
In 1006 he was murdered at Æthelred's order and his sons blinded.
His death widened the gulf between the north and the king.
RULER_UHTRED_BIO:
Lord of Bamburgh and then earl of all Northumbria 1006–1016.
He beat the Scots at Durham and won Æthelred's daughter in marriage.
In 1016 he submitted to Cnut, and was cut down at the parley.
His killing began a long blood feud in the house of Bamburgh.
RULER_EADULF_CUDEL_BIO:
Uhtred's brother, lord of Bamburgh after 1016.
The chronicle calls him a coward: “cudel” means soft.
Fearing the Scots, he ceded Lothian to them.
So the Tweed became the border, and the border it stayed.
RULER_SIWARD_BIO:
An earl of Danish stock, lord of Northumbria 1033–1055.
He killed his rival Eadulf and so joined York and Bamburgh under one hand.
In 1054 he marched into Scotland and defeated Macbeth.
Told his son had fallen, he asked only whether the wound was in front.
RULER_TOSTIG_BIO:
Son of Godwin, Earl of Northumbria 1055–1065, brother of Harold.
His harsh taxes and judgements drove the north into revolt.
The king outlawed him, and his brother did not stand by him.
In 1066 he came back with Harald of Norway and fell at Stamford Bridge.
RULER_MORCAR_BIO:
Son of Ælfgar, Earl of Northumbria from 1065, chosen by the rebels.
At Fulford he was beaten alongside his brother Edwin.
He submitted to William, then joined Hereward at Ely.
He spent the rest of his life in Norman captivity.
RULER_AETHELSTAN_HALFKING_BIO:
Ealdorman of East Anglia 932–956; his byname came from his power.
Half the realm lay under him and his kinsmen.
The future King Edgar was brought up in his own household.
At the height of his power he entered the abbey of Glastonbury by choice.
RULER_AETHELWINE_BIO:
Son of the Half-King, ealdorman of East Anglia 962–992.
He was called “God's friend” for his generosity to the monasteries.
He founded Ramsey and defended monastic lands against Ælfhere.
After he died East Anglia stood in the front line of the Viking attacks.
RULER_THORKELL_BIO:
Leader of the Jomsvikings and Earl of East Anglia under Cnut.
From 1009 he terrorised England, then took Æthelred's pay.
His men killed Archbishop Ælfheah in 1012 though he forbade it.
Cnut first made him earl, then outlawed him, then set him over Denmark.
RULER_HAROLD_GODWINSON_BIO:
Son of Godwin, Earl of East Anglia and then of Wessex; the future Harold II.
After his father's death he was the strongest man in England after the king.
In 1063 he and his brother broke the power of Gruffydd of Wales.
When Edward the Confessor died the witan chose him as king.
RULER_GYRTH_BIO:
Son of Godwin, Earl of East Anglia from 1057, brother of Harold.
Before Hastings he urged that the king himself should not lead the army.
In the battle he fought beside his brother under the banner.
He fell on the hill together with Harold and Leofwine.
RULER_GORM_BIO:
The first securely known member of the Danish royal house, lord of Jelling.
He raised the smaller Jelling rune-stone for his wife Thyra.
Tradition holds that he stayed a heathen to the end.
His son Harald Bluetooth had him reburied as a Christian.
RULER_HARALD_BLUETOOTH_BIO:
King of the Danes from 958; the Jelling stones boast of his deeds.
He had it carved in stone that he “made the Danes Christian”.
He built the ring fortresses (Trelleborg) and for a time ruled Norway too.
His own son Sweyn rebelled and drove him from the throne.
RULER_HARALD_II_DK_BIO:
Elder son of Sweyn Forkbeard, King of the Danes 1014–1018.
When his father died he stayed at home while his brother fought for England.
In his short reign Denmark kept out of the English wars.
At his death his brother Cnut joined the two crowns.
RULER_MAGNUS_BIO:
Son of St Olaf, King of Norway (1035) and of Denmark (1042).
A treaty of mutual inheritance made him king of the Danes.
At Lyrskov Heath he crushed the Wends attacking from the south.
He died young in 1047, and had laid claim to England too.
RULER_SWEYN_ESTRIDSEN_BIO:
Son of Cnut's sister, King of the Danes 1047–1076.
He warred fifteen years with Harald Hardrada before peace came.
In 1069 he sent a fleet against Norman England.
Every later Danish king descends from him.
RULER_HARALD_III_DK_BIO:
Son of Sweyn Estridsen, King of the Danes 1076–1080.
His byname “Hein” means whetstone — a mild, yielding king.
He made laws that shielded the poorer sort.
After his short reign his brother Canute followed him.
RULER_CANUTE_IV_BIO:
King of the Danes 1080–1086, and Denmark's first saint.
He meant to win England back and gathered a great fleet.
The farmers tired of waiting and of the levies, and rose against him.
He was killed in Odense, before the altar of the church.
RULER_OLAF_I_DK_BIO:
Brother of St Canute, King of the Danes 1086–1095.
His byname is “Hunger”: famine struck the land for years under him.
The people held that the curse of a brother's death lay on the soil.
After he died his brother was canonised — and the harvests came back.
RULER_ROLLO_BIO:
A Viking leader to whom the Frankish king gave land at the Seine mouth in 911.
The treaty of Saint-Clair-sur-Epte made him the first lord of Normandy.
He was baptised as Robert and became father of the ducal line.
William the Conqueror descends from him in the direct line.
RULER_WILLIAM_LONGSWORD_BIO:
Son of Rollo, lord of Normandy 927–942.
He pushed towards Brittany and served at the Frankish royal court.
He had to govern lords who still spoke Norse on Norman soil.
In 942 he was lured to a meeting on the river and killed.
RULER_RICHARD_I_BIO:
Lord of Normandy 942–996, for more than fifty years.
He inherited as a child and had to be smuggled out of the Frankish king's keeping.
With Danish help he threw back the Franks who coveted the duchy.
In his long reign the Normans became French for good.
RULER_RICHARD_II_BIO:
Duke of Normandy 996–1026; the first to use the ducal title.
He married his sister Emma to Æthelred II of England.
Out of that match grew the Norman claim to the English throne.
His harbours were open to the fleets coming from Denmark.
RULER_RICHARD_III_BIO:
Duke of Normandy 1026–1027, for barely a year.
His brother Robert rebelled at once and had to be put down.
After the settlement he died with suspicious suddenness.
More than one contemporary blamed his brother for it.
RULER_ROBERT_I_BIO:
Duke of Normandy 1027–1035, father of William the Conqueror.
He took in the exiled English princes Edward and Alfred.
He gathered a fleet to restore them, but the wind scattered it.
He died in 1035 on his way home from pilgrimage to the Holy Land.
RULER_ROBERT_CURTHOSE_BIO:
Eldest son of the Conqueror, Duke of Normandy 1087–1106.
He took up arms against his own father over the duchy.
He fought at Jerusalem as one of the leaders of the First Crusade.
His brother Henry I beat him and held him prisoner till he died.
RULER_SIGFRED_HALFDAN_DK_BIO:
Two brothers who shared the Danish kingship in the 870s.
One stayed at home while the other harried the Frankish coasts.
A Frankish envoy recorded that they ruled together.
In those years the Danish throne was rarely held by one man alone.
RULER_OLOF_DK_BIO:
A king out of Sweden who ruled Hedeby in the early 900s.
A German chronicler says a foreign house then sat on the Danish throne.
His sons Gnupa and Gurd followed him in power.
His rule shows how weak the Danish kingship then was.
RULER_GNUPA_DK_BIO:
Son of Olof, king at Hedeby in the 920s.
A campaign by King Henry I of Germany forced him to submit.
He had to accept baptism and pay tribute.
His wife Ásfríðr raised two rune-stones in his memory.
RULER_SEINE_VIKINGS_BIO:
The leaders of the Viking hosts that ravaged the Seine in the late 800s.
Sidroc, Weland and their like served now each other, now the Frankish king.
They besieged Paris and wrung out enormous ransoms.
They built no realm: they lived from one campaign to the next.
RULER_IMAR_BIO:
King of Dublin and forefather of the mighty Uí Ímair kindred.
Many identify him with Ivar of the great Danish army.
He raided the coasts of Ireland and Scotland alike.
He died in 873 styled “king of the Norsemen of all Ireland and Britain”.
RULER_OISTIN_BIO:
Son of Amlaíb, king in Dublin in the early 870s.
He led the city's warriors while his father was away.
In 875 he was killed in Alba, by the hand of Albann.
After his death a war among kinsmen broke out for Dublin.
RULER_SICHFRITH_BIO:
Son of Ímar, king of Dublin in the 880s.
He fought his own kinsmen for the town.
In 888 he fell by his brother's hand.
In those years the throne of Dublin rarely stayed in one hand ten years.
RULER_SITRIUC_I_BIO:
Son of Ímar, king of Dublin after 888.
He fought and traded by turns with the Irish kingdoms around him.
In 896 his own kinsmen killed him.
In his day Dublin was already a rich port town.
RULER_DUBLIN_EXILE_BIO:
In 902 the Irish stormed Dublin and drove out its Norse kings.
The fugitives sought new lands in Britain and on Man.
For fifteen years there was no Norse king in Dublin.
They came back in 917 and took the town again.
RULER_GUTHFRITH_BIO:
Kinsman of Ragnall, King of Dublin 921–934.
In 927 he tried to take York, but Æthelstan drove him off.
He also fought the Norse of Limerick for mastery of the sea.
His son Olaf came back in 937 to the field of Brunanburh.
RULER_OLAF_CUARAN_BIO:
Son of Sihtric; king in Dublin and York across more than forty years.
Twice he ruled at York, and twice he was baptised.
In 980 Máel Sechnaill II defeated him at Tara.
After that he withdrew to Iona and died there a monk.
RULER_SIGTRYGG_SILKBEARD_BIO:
King of Dublin for nearly fifty years (989–1036).
The first coins ever struck in Ireland were struck in his reign.
At Clontarf in 1014 he watched the battle from the town walls.
He also founded Christ Church cathedral in the city.
RULER_ECHMARCACH_BIO:
King of Man and the Isles, and twice lord of Dublin as well.
He ruled on the meeting-line of the Irish, Norse and Scottish worlds.
He met Cnut when the northern kings did homage at Rome.
He died in Rome in 1064, on pilgrimage.
RULER_GODRED_CROVAN_BIO:
King of Man and the Isles from 1079, a survivor of Stamford Bridge.
It took him three attempts to conquer the Isle of Man.
He seized Dublin too and controlled the sea roads.
The whole later house of the kings of the Isles descends from him.
RULER_RHODRI_AP_MERFYN_BIO:
King of Gwynedd 844–878, later called “the Great”.
By inheritance and marriage Powys and Seisyllwg fell to him as well.
In 856 he killed the Danish leader Gorm, and word of it reached the Frankish court.
He fell in 878 fighting the Mercians.
RULER_ANARAWD_BIO:
Son of Rhodri, King of Gwynedd 878–916.
At the Conwy in 881 he avenged his father's death on the Mercians.
He first allied with the Norse of York, then turned to Alfred.
Under the protection of Wessex he kept his kingdom.
RULER_IDWAL_FOEL_BIO:
Son of Anarawd, King of Gwynedd 916–942.
He appeared more than once as a witness at Æthelstan's court.
In the end he rose against English overlordship.
He fell fighting the English in 942, together with his sons.
RULER_HYWEL_DDA_BIO:
King of Deheubarth and then Gwynedd; called “the Good” for his laws.
The gathering of the Welsh laws is linked to his name.
He went on pilgrimage to Rome and struck his own coin.
After 942 he held more of Wales than any man of his day.
RULER_IAGO_AB_IDWAL_BIO:
Son of Idwal Foel, King of Gwynedd from 950, at first with his brother.
The brothers soon turned on each other.
His own son seized him and put him in prison.
At the end of his reign Danish raids reached Anglesey too.
RULER_MAREDUDD_BIO:
King of Deheubarth and Gwynedd 986–999, grandson of Hywel the Good.
He gathered much of Wales into one hand again.
He paid the Vikings a huge ransom for captives they had carried off.
After his death his kingdom fell apart once more.
RULER_CYNAN_AP_HYWEL_BIO:
King of Gwynedd 999–1005, of the northern house.
He tried to hold the throne in an age of endless feuding.
The sources have kept almost nothing of him.
After his death Llywelyn ap Seisyll took power.
RULER_LLYWELYN_AP_SEISYLL_BIO:
King of Gwynedd and Deheubarth 1018–1023.
He won the northern kingdom through his marriage.
A chronicle says that in his day “there was no want in Wales”.
His son was the later Gruffydd ap Llywelyn.
RULER_IAGO_AB_IDWAL_MEURIG_BIO:
King of Gwynedd 1023–1039, the last strong man of the old northern house.
He won back the family throne after Llywelyn's death.
His own men killed him in 1039.
After him Gruffydd ap Llywelyn seized power.
RULER_GRUFFYDD_AP_LLYWELYN_BIO:
The one ruler who united the whole of Wales (1055–1063).
He took Gwynedd first, then the other kingdoms one by one.
Allied with Earl Ælfgar, he burned Hereford.
Fleeing Harold's campaign in 1063, he was killed by his own men.
RULER_BLEDDYN_BIO:
Half-brother of Gruffydd, King of Gwynedd and Powys 1063–1075.
The English gave him the northern throne after his brother fell.
He joined the northern rising against the Normans in 1069.
His own kinsmen killed him; he was remembered as a renewer of Welsh law.
RULER_TRAHAEARN_BIO:
King of Gwynedd 1075–1081, cousin of Bleddyn.
He defended his throne against the Norman marcher lords and rival claimants.
He fell in 1081 on the field of Mynydd Carn.
With him the Powys branch at the head of Gwynedd died out.
RULER_GRUFFUDD_AP_CYNAN_BIO:
Born in Dublin, King of Gwynedd from 1081, with long interruptions.
He came back to his fathers' land with a Norse-Irish fleet.
He spent twelve years in Norman captivity at Chester.
Once free, he held Gwynedd to the end of his life.
RULER_HARALD_FAIRHAIR_BIO:
By tradition the first to unite Norway, about 871.
The saga says he vowed not to cut his hair until it was done.
At Hafrsfjord he beat the league of the petty kings.
The chieftains who fled him settled Iceland.
RULER_HAAKON_GOOD_BIO:
Youngest son of Harald Fairhair, King of Norway 934–961.
He was raised a Christian in England, at Æthelstan's court.
He organised the fleet levy and coastal watch (leiðangr).
His faith was never accepted; he died of a wound taken at Fitjar.
RULER_HARALD_GREYCLOAK_BIO:
Son of Eric Bloodaxe, King of Norway 961–970.
He and his brothers took the throne with Danish backing.
He struck hard at the heathen sacrifices and so lost all liking.
He was lured into a trap in Denmark and killed.
RULER_HAAKON_JARL_BIO:
Jarl of Lade and the real ruler of Norway 970–995.
First the Danish king's deputy, he then made himself independent.
At Hjörungavágr he threw back the attack of the Jomsvikings.
The last great defender of the old rites, he was killed by his own thrall.
RULER_OLAF_TRYGGVASON_BIO:
King of Norway 995–1000, risen to the throne out of a Viking past.
He took tribute from England, then was baptised and sailed home.
By sword and fire he converted much of Norway.
In the sea-battle of Svolder he leapt into the water and was never seen again.
RULER_ERIC_JARL_BIO:
Son of Jarl Haakon, ruler of Norway 1000–1015 under Danish overlordship.
At Svolder he led the winning fleet against Olaf.
He helped Cnut conquer England.
He died in England as Earl of Northumbria.
RULER_OLAF_SAINT_BIO:
King of Norway 1015–1028, its eternal king and patron saint.
He grew up on campaigns in England, then came home and took the throne.
His hard hand and Cnut's gold together drove the chieftains to expel him.
He fell at Stiklestad in 1030 and was soon venerated as a saint.
RULER_HARALD_HARDRADA_BIO:
Half-brother of St Olaf, King of Norway 1046–1066; “the hard ruler”.
As a young man he served in the Varangian Guard of the Byzantine emperor.
For fifteen years he warred for Denmark, then turned on England.
He fell at Stamford Bridge in 1066 — with him the Viking age ended.
RULER_MAGNUS_II_NO_BIO:
Son of Harald Hardrada, King of Norway 1066–1069.
While his father campaigned in England he stayed home to govern.
After the defeat he shared the throne with his brother Olaf.
He died young three years later.
RULER_OLAF_KYRRE_BIO:
Son of Harald Hardrada, King of Norway 1066–1093, for nearly thirty years.
After Stamford Bridge he made peace and sailed home with what was left of the fleet.
In his whole reign he fought no great war.
He founded towns (Bergen) and set up bishoprics.
RULER_MAGNUS_BAREFOOT_BIO:
Son of Olaf the Peaceful, King of Norway 1093–1103; the last king of the old Viking expeditions.
His byname came from the Gaelic dress he wore in the Scottish isles.
He renewed Norwegian rule over Man, the Hebrides and Orkney.
He fell in Ireland in 1103, cut down from ambush.
RULER_BEORHTRIC_BIO:
King of Wessex 786–802, ally and son-in-law of Offa of Mercia.
In his reign the first Viking ships put in at Portland.
The king's reeve who challenged them was killed on the spot.
Tradition says his own wife poisoned him by accident.
RULER_EGBERT_W_BIO:
King of Wessex 802–839 and forefather of the later English royal house.
As a young man he lived in exile at Charlemagne's court.
At Ellendun in 825 he beat Mercia and won the south-east.
In 829 he was for a short while overlord of all England.
RULER_AETHELWULF_BIO:
Son of Egbert, King of Wessex 839–858 and father of Alfred.
In 851 he won a great victory over the Danes at Aclea.
He went on pilgrimage to Rome with his son and gave lavishly.
On his return his own son rebelled and he had to share his power.
RULER_AETHELBALD_BIO:
Son of Æthelwulf, King of Wessex 858–860.
He rebelled in his father's lifetime and forced a division of the realm.
After his father's death he married the old king's young widow.
The match caused scandal, and two years later he was dead.
RULER_AETHELBERHT_W_BIO:
Son of Æthelwulf, King of Wessex 860–865.
Under him Wessex and Kent were joined in one kingdom again.
A Danish force took and plundered Winchester.
The local ealdormen drove the raiders back.
RULER_AETHELRED_I_W_BIO:
Son of Æthelwulf, King of Wessex 865–871 and Alfred's brother.
In his reign the great Danish army came to the island.
He won at Ashdown but was beaten at Basing and Meretun.
He died of his wounds after Easter, and his brother followed him.
RULER_OFFA_BIO:
King of Mercia 757–796, the mightiest English ruler of the age.
Charlemagne wrote to him as an equal.
Offa's Dyke, the great earthwork on the Welsh border, bears his name.
He struck the silver penny and had his son crowned king in his own lifetime.
RULER_ECGFRITH_M_BIO:
Son of Offa, King of Mercia in 796 for only a few months.
His father had him crowned in his own lifetime to make the succession safe.
Alcuin wrote that he paid with an early death for his father's sins.
After him the Mercian kingship passed to another branch.
RULER_COENWULF_BIO:
King of Mercia 796–821, heir to Offa's power.
He crushed the revolt in Kent and captured King Eadberht Præn.
He quarrelled for years with the Archbishop of Canterbury over church rights.
With his death Mercia's leading role began to fade.
RULER_CEOLWULF_I_BIO:
Brother of Coenwulf, King of Mercia 821–823.
In the Welsh war he destroyed the fortress of Deganwy in Powys.
Two years later the Mercian magnates deposed him.
With his fall the feuding of the royal house became permanent.
RULER_BEORNWULF_BIO:
King of Mercia 823–826, not of the old royal line.
At Ellendun in 825 Egbert dealt him a ruinous defeat.
After it Kent, Sussex and Essex broke away from Mercia.
He fell in East Anglia while trying to win it back.
RULER_LUDECA_BIO:
King of Mercia 826–827, after Beornwulf's fall.
He sat on the throne barely a year.
He fell in East Anglia together with five of his ealdormen.
He died on the very campaign that had killed his predecessor.
RULER_WIGLAF_BIO:
King of Mercia 827–829 and again 830–840.
Egbert drove him out for a year, but he won his throne back.
In his second reign Mercia was independent once more.
He was buried at Repton, the burial place of the Mercian kings.
RULER_BEORHTWULF_BIO:
King of Mercia 840–852.
He sought alliance with Wessex against the Danish fleets.
In 851 the Danes beat his army at London.
After him his son-in-law Burgred took the throne.
RULER_UNDER_MERCIA_BIO:
This land has no king of its own at present.
The ruler of Mercia governs it through sub-kings or ealdormen.
The local house at most receives the title of sub-king.
Its dues and its levies serve the Mercian king.
RULER_AETHELRED_I_N_BIO:
King of Northumbria 774–779 and again 790–796.
He came back from exile and took bloody vengeance on his rivals.
In his reign the Vikings sacked the monastery of Lindisfarne (793).
His own men killed him in 796.
RULER_EARDWULF_BIO:
King of Northumbria 796–806 and again 808–810.
He had once been left for dead at an execution, and men held it a miracle.
He warred with Mercia, then returned with the help of Charlemagne and the pope.
His reign is the last reasonably firm period of the Northumbrian kingdom.
RULER_AELFWALD_II_BIO:
King of Northumbria 806–808, after Eardwulf was driven out.
He held the throne barely two years.
He struck his own coin, but little else of him survives.
He vanishes from the sources when Eardwulf returned.
RULER_EANRED_BIO:
Son of Eardwulf, King of Northumbria 810–841, for over thirty years.
His long reign brought the northern kingdom a rare calm.
The Chronicle says he bowed to Egbert and took him as his lord.
His coinage was already debased, copper mixed into the silver.
RULER_AETHELRED_II_N_BIO:
Son of Eanred, King of Northumbria 841–848, with a break.
A usurper named Rædwulf drove him out for a time.
Rædwulf fell fighting the Vikings, so he could return.
In the end his own men murdered him too.
RULER_OSBERHT_BIO:
King of Northumbria from 848 until 862 or 867.
At the end of his reign the kingdom split between him and Ælla.
In 867 they nevertheless joined forces against the Danes.
He fell beneath the walls of York together with Ælla.
RULER_AELLE_II_BIO:
King of Northumbria in 862/867; the Chronicle says he was of no royal blood.
The great Danish army took York in 866.
He fell in March 867 in the attempt to retake it.
Later saga says Ragnar's sons killed him in revenge.
RULER_AETHELBERHT_EA_BIO:
King of East Anglia 779–794.
He struck his own coin, a denial of Offa's overlordship.
He was beheaded at Offa's court, supposedly on a charge of treason.
He was venerated as a saint at Hereford, whose cathedral bears his name.
RULER_EADWALD_BIO:
King of East Anglia about 796, after Offa's death.
He seized the moment when Mercian power faltered.
For a short time he struck his own coin.
Coenwulf restored Mercian rule, and he disappeared.
RULER_ATHELSTAN_EA_BIO:
King of East Anglia from about 827, after shaking off Mercian rule.
In his time two Mercian kings fell in the eastern lands.
He turned to Egbert of Wessex for protection.
With him the independent kingdom of East Anglia revived.
RULER_AETHELWEARD_EA_BIO:
King of East Anglia about 845.
He is known only from coins and a few charters.
He ruled the last peaceful decade of the independent kingdom.
His successor Edmund met the great Danish army.
RULER_EDMUND_MARTYR_EA_BIO:
The last independent king of East Anglia, 855–869.
In 869 the great Danish army beat him and took him captive.
Tradition says he was shot with arrows for refusing to deny his faith.
His shrine at Bury St Edmunds became one of England's greatest pilgrim sites.
RULER_OFFA_KENT_BIO:
After 785 Kent had no sub-king of its own: Offa ruled it directly.
The Mercian king himself issued the charters for Kentish land.
He even tried to recast the rank of Canterbury to his own advantage.
The men of Kent never accepted it: they rose the moment he died.
RULER_EADBERHT_PRAEN_BIO:
King of Kent 796–798, raised up by revolt after Offa's death.
He is said to have been ordained a priest before returning to worldly power.
Coenwulf crushed the rising in 798 and took him prisoner.
He was blinded and maimed; Kentish independence fell with him.
RULER_CUTHRED_BIO:
Brother of Coenwulf, sub-king of Kent 798–807.
His brother set him on the Kentish throne after the revolt was crushed.
He struck his own coin but followed Mercia in everything.
After his death Coenwulf appointed no new sub-king.
RULER_BALDRED_BIO:
The last king of Kent, 823–825.
He tried to rule on his own as Mercia weakened.
In 825 Egbert's son Æthelwulf drove him beyond the Thames.
Kent thereafter belonged to Wessex.
RULER_AETHELWULF_KENT_BIO:
Son of Egbert, sub-king of Kent 825–839.
His father sent him to conquer the south-eastern kingdoms.
Kent, Surrey, Sussex and Essex came under his rule.
On his father's death he became King of Wessex.
RULER_AETHELSTAN_KENT_BIO:
Son of Æthelwulf, sub-king of Kent 839–852.
At Sandwich in 851 he won a sea-fight against the Danes.
He took nine ships — the first recorded English victory at sea.
He died young, in his father's lifetime.
RULER_AETHELBERHT_KENT_BIO:
Son of Æthelwulf, sub-king of Kent 852–860.
He received the south-eastern kingdoms after his brother's death.
In 860 he became King of Wessex and kept Kent in his own hand.
With him the separate Kentish sub-kingship ended for good.
RULER_SIGERIC_BIO:
King of Essex 758–798, of the old house of the East Saxons.
He ruled under Mercian overlordship, as a sub-king.
In 798 he gave up the throne and went as a pilgrim to Rome.
His son Sigered followed him, with ever less power.
RULER_SIGERED_BIO:
The last king of Essex from 798, the last ruler of the East Saxon house.
His title sank from king to sub-king and then to ealdorman.
The Mercian charters demoted him step by step.
After 825 Essex passed to Wessex and the old kingdom was no more.
RULER_SUSSEX_DUCES_BIO:
After 772 Sussex had no king of its own.
Offa's charters call its lords duces, that is ealdormen.
The land of the South Saxons became a Mercian province.
In 825 Sussex went over to Wessex, and there it stayed.
RULER_DONNCOIRCE_BIO:
King of Dál Riata in the 780s.
The Gaelic kingdom already lived in the shadow of the Picts.
The Irish annals record his death in a single line.
After him nothing certain is known of the throne for decades.
RULER_DALRIATA_UNKNOWN_BIO:
Decades from which no king's name of Dál Riata survives.
The annals of those years speak of Picts and Vikings instead.
The Gaelic lords either submitted or withdrew to Ireland.
Out of this darkness the house of Cináed mac Ailpín would rise.
RULER_CONALL_MAC_TAIDG_BIO:
King of Dál Riata and for a time of the Picts in the early 800s.
The two thrones were then beginning to entwine.
His rival Conall mac Áedáin drove him out in 807.
He fell in Kintyre that same year, a victim of the feud.
RULER_CONALL_MAC_AEDAIN_BIO:
King of Dál Riata about 807, after beating his rival.
Almost nothing survives of his short reign.
The Irish annals know him from a single entry.
After him the Pictish Caustantín took the Gaelic kingdom as well.
RULER_CAUSTANTIN_MAC_FERGUSA_BIO:
King of the Picts 789–820, and for a time of Dál Riata too.
In his reign the great Viking attacks on Iona began.
He founded the church at Dunkeld, where Iona's relics were brought for safety.
Under him the Pictish and Gaelic kingships grew together.
RULER_OENGUS_II_BIO:
Brother of Caustantín, King of the Picts 820–834.
Tradition makes him the founder of the church at St Andrews.
Legend ties the saltire in the sky to one of his battles.
After him the Pictish kingdom fell quickly into decline.
RULER_AED_MAC_BOANTA_BIO:
King of Dál Riata in the 830s.
He fell in 839 in the great battle against the Vikings.
The Pictish king died in that same fight.
The Gaelic and Pictish leading men perished there together.
RULER_EOGANAN_BIO:
King of the Picts and of Dál Riata 837–839.
He fell in 839, with his brother, fighting the Vikings.
The flower of the Pictish nobility perished in that defeat.
That battle opened the way for Cináed mac Ailpín.
RULER_CINAED_MAC_AILPIN_BIO:
King of Dál Riata and from 843 of the Picts; by tradition the founder of Scotland.
He took over a Pictish power mauled by the Vikings.
He brought Iona's relics to Dunkeld and made it a church centre.
His heirs became kings of Alba: the Scottish king-list begins with him.
RULER_DOMNALL_I_BIO:
Brother of Cináed, King of the Picts 858–862.
Tradition says he extended the laws of Dál Riata over the whole realm.
In his short reign the Vikings attacked without pause.
He died at Scone, the place where kings were made.
RULER_CAUSANTIN_I_BIO:
Son of Cináed, King of the Picts 862–877.
In his reign the Dublin armies of Amlaíb and Ímar harried the land.
In 870 Dumbarton, the British capital of Strathclyde, fell.
He himself died in 877 fighting the Vikings.
RULER_AED_ALBA_BIO:
Son of Cináed, King of the Picts 877–878, barely a year.
He came to the throne for a short while after his brother's death.
His kinsman Giric killed him in a war within the family.
His son became Causantín II, the long-reigning king.
RULER_GIRIC_BIO:
King of Alba 878–889, perhaps jointly with Eochaid.
Later tradition credits him with freeing the Scottish church.
Some sources call him “conqueror of Britain”.
He died at the time of an eclipse, and the chronicles say he was driven out.
RULER_DOMNALL_II_BIO:
Son of Causantín I, King of Alba 889–900.
He is the first called “king of Alba” rather than of the Picts.
In his reign the Vikings once more ravaged the land.
He died at Dunnottar, perhaps in battle.
RULER_CAUSANTIN_II_BIO:
King of Alba 900–943, for more than forty years.
At Corbridge in 918 he barred the way of the Norse of York.
At Brunanburh in 937 he fought Æthelstan, and his son fell there.
He abdicated of his own will and died a monk at St Andrews.
RULER_MAEL_COLUIM_I_BIO:
Son of Domnall I, King of Alba 943–954.
Edmund I gave him Strathclyde in return for alliance.
He campaigned against Moray and struggled with the northern lords.
The men of the north killed him in 954.
RULER_ILDULB_BIO:
Son of Causantín II, King of Alba 954–962.
In his time Edinburgh came into Scottish hands.
That was the first great step towards winning Lothian.
He fell fighting the Vikings.
RULER_DUB_BIO:
Son of Máel Coluim I, King of Alba 962–967.
The two branches of the royal house fought over the throne.
Cuilén drove him out, and the men of Moray killed him.
Tradition says his body was hidden under a bridge.
RULER_CUILEN_BIO:
Son of Ildulb, King of Alba 967–971.
He won the throne by driving out his rival.
The Britons of Strathclyde killed him in 971.
The sources say the vengeance came over a carried-off girl.
RULER_CINAED_II_BIO:
Son of Máel Coluim I, King of Alba 971–995.
He led raids into England and into Strathclyde.
Tradition says he changed the rule of succession.
His own men lured him into a trap and killed him at Fettercairn.
RULER_CAUSANTIN_III_BIO:
Son of Cuilén, King of Alba 995–997, barely two years.
He was one more figure in the bloody alternation of the two branches.
He fell in the fighting over the throne.
After his death the other branch took the crown.
RULER_CINAED_III_BIO:
Son of Dub, King of Alba 997–1005.
He came to the throne by killing his predecessor.
He fell at Monzievaird against Máel Coluim II.
With him the generations-long feud of the two branches ended.
RULER_MAEL_COLUIM_II_BIO:
Son of Cináed II, King of Alba 1005–1034, for nearly thirty years.
His victory at Carham in 1018 made Lothian Scottish for good.
He left Strathclyde to his grandson too: the shape of Scotland was set.
He died without a son, so his grandson Donnchad followed him.
RULER_DONNCHAD_I_BIO:
Grandson of Máel Coluim II, King of Alba 1034–1040.
He was young, and his short reign brought only failed campaigns.
The siege of Durham ended in heavy defeat.
Macbeth killed him in battle in 1040 — not in bed, as the play has it.
RULER_MAC_BETHAD_BIO:
Lord of Moray, King of Alba 1040–1057; the Macbeth of the play.
In truth he ruled seventeen years, and the land was quiet.
In 1050 he went on pilgrimage to Rome and “scattered money like seed”.
He fell at Lumphanan against Máel Coluim III.
RULER_LULACH_BIO:
Macbeth's stepson, King of Alba 1057–1058, for a few months.
His byname is “the foolish” or “the unfortunate”.
He is the first Scottish king certainly crowned at Scone.
Seven months later Máel Coluim III killed him by treachery.
RULER_MAEL_COLUIM_III_BIO:
Son of Donnchad I, King of Alba 1058–1093; “Canmore”, the great chief.
He came back from exile in England to avenge his father.
His second wife was the Saxon Margaret, later made a saint.
He invaded England five times, and fell at last near Alnwick.
RULER_DOMNALL_BAN_BIO:
Brother of Máel Coluim III, King of Alba from 1093, with interruptions.
He stood for the old Gaelic order and drove out his brother's English and Norman court.
He had to fight both his nephews and the king of England.
He died at last in captivity, blinded.
RULER_DREST_TALORGAN_BIO:
Two Pictish kings who ruled together about 834.
They rose out of the confusion after great Óengus died.
Their rule lasted only a few years.
Even the Pictish king-lists disagree about them.
RULER_FERAT_BIO:
King of the Picts 839–842, after the great defeat by the Vikings.
He tried to hold together what was left of a shattered kingdom.
In three years he could not make his power firm.
After him his sons and Cináed mac Ailpín contended for the throne.
RULER_BRIDEI_CINIOD_BIO:
Sons of Uurad and the last kings of the Picts, about 842–843.
They ruled one after the other, each only briefly, after their father died.
The Pictish king-list ends with them.
After them Cináed mac Ailpín took the throne and a new age began.
RULER_DONNCHAD_MIDI_BIO:
High King of Tara 770–797, head of the Clann Cholmáin.
He dealt harshly with the rival Irish kingdoms.
He ravaged Leinster again and again, sparing not even churches.
In his reign the first Viking raids struck Ireland.
RULER_AED_OIRDNIDE_BIO:
High King of Ireland 797–819, of the northern Uí Néill.
His byname means “the ordained”: perhaps he was consecrated by the church.
He split Leinster in two to weaken it.
He died in 819 while crossing a river.
RULER_CONCHOBAR_MAC_DONNCHADA_BIO:
Son of Donnchad Midi, High King of Ireland 819–833.
He gained the throne by the alternation of Clann Cholmáin and the northern Uí Néill.
In his reign the Vikings began to set up permanent camps on the coasts.
Armagh and the great monasteries were fought over as well.
RULER_NIALL_CAILLE_BIO:
High King of Ireland 833–846, of the northern Uí Néill.
He faced the Vikings directly and beat them in several fights.
His victories in the north slowed their advance inland.
He drowned in a flooded river while trying to save a man.
RULER_MAEL_SECHNAILL_I_BIO:
High King of Ireland 846–862, head of Clann Cholmáin.
He fought the Vikings and rival Irish kings at the same time.
In 860 he led an army drawn from all Ireland against the north.
He was the first high king acknowledged by nearly the whole island.
RULER_AED_FINDLIATH_BIO:
High King of Ireland 862–879, of the northern Uí Néill.
In 866 he swept the Viking camps of the north and burned them all.
That cleared the northern coasts for decades.
He also fought the Ulaid and Leinster for overlordship.
RULER_FLANN_SINNA_BIO:
High King of Ireland 879–916, for nearly forty years.
His reign marks the height of Clann Cholmáin power.
He raised a great carved cross at Clonmacnoise bearing his name.
His own sons rebelled against him before he died.
RULER_NIALL_GLUNDUB_BIO:
High King of Ireland 916–919, of the northern Uí Néill.
His byname means “black knee”.
He gathered the Irish kings against the Norsemen of Dublin.
He fell in battle beneath the walls of Dublin in 919.
RULER_DONNCHAD_DONN_BIO:
Son of Flann Sinna, High King of Ireland 919–944.
Dublin's strength peaked in his day and reached out towards York.
He had to fight his own brothers and sons for power.
He held the high kingship for twenty-five years.
RULER_CONGALACH_CNOGBA_BIO:
High King of Ireland 944–956, of the royal house of Brega.
In 944 he sacked and plundered Dublin.
With the Norsemen he sometimes fought and sometimes allied.
In 956 the Dubliners killed him from ambush.
RULER_DOMNALL_UA_NEILL_BIO:
High King of Ireland 956–980, of the northern Uí Néill.
He spent his whole reign campaigning, with little to show for it.
He even raised a fleet on the Shannon.
He died at Armagh in monastic penance.
RULER_MAEL_SECHNAILL_II_BIO:
High King of Ireland 980–1002 and again 1014–1022.
At Tara in 980 he beat the Norsemen of Dublin and broke their power.
He yielded the high kingship to Brian Bóruma, and took it back after his death.
He fought on the winning side at Clontarf as well.
RULER_BRIAN_BORU_BIO:
King of Munster and then High King of Ireland 1002–1014.
He broke the centuries-old monopoly of the Uí Néill.
An entry at Armagh calls him “emperor of the Irish”.
He won at Clontarf in 1014 but was killed in his tent after the battle.
RULER_IRISH_CONTESTED_BIO:
The age of “kings with opposition” after 1022.
Several provincial kings claimed the title, but none could hold it alone.
Munster, Connacht and Leinster rose and fell by turns.
This division lasted until the coming of the Normans.
RULER_TOIRDELBACH_UA_BRIAIN_BIO:
Grandson of Brian Bóruma, King of Munster and from 1072 ruler of Ireland.
He brought Dublin and Leinster under his hand.
Pope Gregory VII wrote to him as “king of the Irish”.
His last years were spent in sickness while his sons shared his power.
RULER_MUIRCHERTACH_UA_BRIAIN_BIO:
Son of Toirdelbach, King of Munster and from 1086 ruler of Ireland.
He married his daughter to the king of Man and the Isles.
He gave the rock of Cashel to the church and called synods.
He also made alliance with Magnus Barefoot of Norway.
RULER_CARADOG_AP_MEIRION_BIO:
King of Gwynedd 754–798, of the old northern house.
In his reign Offa of Mercia broke into Wales more than once.
The English killed him near Rhuddlan in 798.
With his death the old male line in Gwynedd died out.
RULER_CYNAN_DINDAETHWY_BIO:
King of Gwynedd 798–816.
He spent almost his whole reign at war with his own kin.
His struggle with Hywel drove him from the throne twice.
He died in exile on the Isle of Man in 816.
RULER_HYWEL_AP_RHODRI_BIO:
King of Gwynedd 816–825, rival and successor of Cynan.
He drove his rival from the island of Anglesey.
In his time the Mercians again broke into Powys.
His death in 825 ended the old house for good.
RULER_MERFYN_FRYCH_BIO:
King of Gwynedd 825–844; he came from Man and inherited through his mother.
With him a new dynasty of Welsh kings begins.
Irish and Frankish scholars passed through his court.
His son was the later Rhodri the Great.
RULER_CHARLEMAGNE_BIO:
King of the Franks from 768 and Roman Emperor from 800.
He gathered most of western Europe into a single empire.
He wrote to Offa as an equal and made a trade agreement with him.
At his court the Anglo-Saxon Alcuin led the school.
RULER_LOUIS_PIOUS_BIO:
Son of Charlemagne, Frankish Emperor 814–840.
He began with church reform and open-handed giving.
His own sons rebelled twice over how the empire should be divided.
After his death the empire broke into three.
RULER_CHARLES_BALD_BIO:
Son of Louis the Pious, King of the West Franks 840–877.
The treaty of Verdun gave him most of what is now France.
Against the Viking fleets he used now silver, now fortified bridges.
In the end he could not hold the mouths of the Seine and the Loire.
RULER_NORSE_SEA_KINGS_BIO:
The age of unnamed Norwegian sea-kings in the 790s.
They ruled no land, only ships and a following.
They went from shore to shore for plunder and sailed home for winter.
Out of them came the later kings of Dublin and the Isles.
RULER_AMLAIB_BIO:
King of Dublin 853–871, the strongest of the Norse sea-kings.
He ruled together with Ímar, and they campaigned together.
In 870 they took Dumbarton, the chief fortress of Strathclyde.
The sources say he went back to Norway and fell there.
RULER_NORWAY_PETTY_KINGS_BIO:
Norway is not yet one realm: each fjord has its own petty king.
The lords of Vestfold, Agder and Hordaland vie with one another.
With their ships they set out west across the sea for plunder.
Harald Fairhair would one day break this order.
RULER_DANES_OVERSEAS_BIO:
At this time the Danes still live overseas, in their own land.
Only small raiding ships cross over to England.
At home Godfred and his heirs build a rampart against the Franks.
The great army will not cross to the island until 865.
RULER_IVAR_BIO:
The leaders of the great Danish army of 865; in tradition the sons of Ragnar.
Ivar's byname “the Boneless” comes from saga; its reason is unknown.
In 869 they killed Edmund, king of East Anglia.
Ubba, tradition says, fell in Devon in 878.
RULER_SIGFRED_DK_BIO:
King of the Danes in the 770s.
The Frankish annals first mention Danish kingship in connection with him.
He gave shelter to the Saxon Widukind, Charlemagne's enemy.
In his reign the Danish-Frankish border quarrels began.
RULER_GODFRED_DK_BIO:
King of the Danes 804–810, Charlemagne's most dangerous northern foe.
He attacked Frisia with two hundred ships and exacted tribute.
The strengthening of the Danevirke rampart is linked to his name.
In 810 one of his own men killed him.
RULER_HEMMING_DK_BIO:
Nephew of Godfred, King of the Danes 810–812.
He made peace with Charlemagne at once.
The river Eider became the border of the two realms.
He died two years later, and civil war broke out over the succession.
RULER_HARALD_KLAK_DK_BIO:
King of the Danes about 812 and again 819–827, with interruptions.
He came back to the throne with the Frankish emperor's backing.
Baptised at Mainz in 826, he was the first Christian king of the Danes.
The Danes drove him out for it, and he was given land in Frisia.
RULER_HORIK_I_DK_BIO:
Son of Godfred, King of the Danes 813–854, for more than forty years.
He began as one of several brothers and ended alone on the throne.
His fleets sailed up the Rhine and the Seine.
In 854 he fell in a battle with his kinsmen, and nearly all his house with him.
RULER_HORIK_II_DK_BIO:
King of the Danes after 854, a kinsman of the previous king.
His byname is “the child”: he came to the throne young.
He let the missionary Ansgar build churches at Hedeby and Ribe.
After him the Danish kingship fades from the sources for a long while.

Win and the army scatters, half of it fleeing home; lose and your garrison bleeds while the army marches on. Each army can be struck once per season.
CHR_AMBUSH_WIN: Ambush near {1}: the marching army of {0} was scattered ({2} against {3}).
CHR_AMBUSH_LOSS: The ambush near {1} failed: the army of {0} marched on ({2} against {3}).

MENU_TUTORIAL_TIP: Walks you through the game: it tells you what to do, shows you where the button is, and you do it yourself. Starts as Wessex. You can leave it at any time.
TUT_1_T:
The year is 790. Britain is split among small kingdoms, and the Vikings will soon arrive from the sea. You are the king of Wessex.

I will walk you through the basics: I tell you what to do, I frame the place on screen where you do it — the rest is up to you. You can leave at any time with Skip or Esc.
TUT_2_T:
The top bar shows the year and season, and how much silver, food and manpower you have. One turn is one season: four turns make a year.

Silver pays for building and recruiting, food keeps your armies alive. If either runs out you are in trouble — the realm table tells you how long they will last.
TUT_3_T:
Your turn: **click one of your own provinces on the map** — yours are shown in your colour.

The chosen province's details appear in the panel on the right. We cannot go on until you pick one.
TUT_4_T:
Here you see the population, the garrison (fyrd and thegns), the defences and the buildings.

The **fyrd** is the called-up peasant levy: plentiful but weak. A **thegn** is a professional warrior: few, but worth much. A **burh** is a fortified town — whoever sits behind one is hard to shift.

Hover a province on the map and it also tells you its terrain: battles in hills, woods or marshes go differently.
TUT_5_T:
These buttons are the province's improvements. **Click one that is not greyed out** — at the very start that means a village or a farm.

Every improvement costs silver, food, timber or iron, and the button shows how much. Where something is not possible, the button tells you what is missing: warriors can only be recruited beside a barracks, ships only in a port.
TUT_6_T:
This button sends an army on its way: select the starting province, press it, then click the destination on the map.

The march takes several turns, and a small soldier marks it on the map. Beware: **an army on the march can be ambushed** — and you can ambush others passing by your own land.
TUT_7_T:
Select a FOREIGN province you border and are at war with, and this button lets you attack.

Two numbers stand on it: your strength and the defender's. The terrain is already counted in — storming hills or marshes costs far more. If your number is lower, do not go: defeat costs you men and stability alike.

War must be declared in diplomacy before you can attack.
TUT_8_T:
**Click the council button.**

The witan is the assembly of your great men. If they are unhappy you collect less tax and recruit with difficulty; a gift can win them over. A king does not rule alone.
TUT_9_T:
**Click the diplomacy button.**

Here you declare war, make peace, arrange marriages or trade agreements. Click a realm and the **🗺 Show on the map** button takes you to where it still holds land.
TUT_10_T:
Your story runs here: battles, buildings, Viking raids, deaths and coronations. If something happened that you missed, look for it here.

The events of real history appear in their own years too — from the sack of Lindisfarne to the Norman conquest.
TUT_11_T:
When you are done, **press the end-turn button**.

Then taxes come in, food is eaten, the neighbouring kings make their moves, armies advance — and the next season begins. That is the rhythm of the game: one turn, one season.
TUT_12_T:
The rest you will learn as you go. Still ahead of you: the coming of the Vikings, the sacking of monasteries, the pope and the quarrels of faith, pretenders to the throne, sea raids, and peace talks where the loser offers tribute or land.

Hover the portrait under the king's name to learn who he was and what he was known for. Rule well!

RULER_KAR_LOTHAIR_I_BIO:
Eldest son of Louis the Pious, co-emperor from 817 and sole holder of the imperial title from 840.
In 841 his brothers Louis the German and Charles the Bald defeated him in the bloody battle of Fontenoy.
The Treaty of Verdun (843) gave him the Middle Kingdom, stretching from Frisia to Italy.
In 855 he gave up his realm and died as a monk in the abbey of Prüm.
RULER_KAR_LOUIS_II_BIO:
Son of Lothair I, king of Italy from 844, co-emperor from 850 and sole emperor from 855.
His power was confined largely to Italy, but there he was an active and forceful ruler.
In 871 he took Bari from the Saracens, but was then briefly held captive by the prince of Benevento.
He died in 875 without a son; Charles the Bald then secured the imperial crown.
RULER_KAR_CHARLES_FAT_BIO:
Youngest son of Louis the German, crowned emperor in Rome in 881.
By 884 deaths in the family let him reunite almost all of Charlemagne's empire for the last time.
At the siege of Paris in 886 he bought the Vikings off with silver and leave to winter in Burgundy.
Deposed in 887 in favour of his nephew Arnulf, he died early in 888.
