RULER_KAR_ARNULF: Arnulf of Carinthia, King of East Francia (Emperor from 896)
RULER_KAR_ARNULF_BIO:
Illegitimate son of Carloman, he seized the East Frankish throne from Charles the Fat in 887.
In 891 he crushed a Viking army on the river Dyle near Leuven.
In 892 he called in the Magyars against Svatopluk of Moravia, one of their earliest mentions in the West.
Crowned emperor in Rome in 896, he soon fell gravely ill and died in 899.
RULER_KAR_LOUIS_CHILD: Louis the Child, King of East Francia
RULER_KAR_LOUIS_CHILD_BIO:
Son of Arnulf, made king in 900 at the age of six; bishops and magnates ruled in his name.
Under him the Magyars destroyed the Bavarian army at Pressburg (Pozsony) in 907.
In 910 his own army was defeated by them near Augsburg.
He died in 911 while still a teenager, the last of the East Frankish Carolingians.
RULER_KAR_CONRAD_I: Conrad I, King of East Francia
RULER_KAR_CONRAD_I_BIO:
Duke of Franconia, elected king in 911, the first East Frankish ruler not of Carolingian blood.
His reign was spent in conflict with the dukes of Saxony, Bavaria and Swabia.
He could not stop the Magyars, who raided as far as Bremen in 915 and Basel in 917.
Dying in 918, he reportedly named his rival, Henry of Saxony, as his successor.
RULER_KAR_HENRY_FOWLER: Henry the Fowler, Duke of Saxony, King of East Francia from 919
RULER_KAR_HENRY_FOWLER_BIO:
Duke of Saxony from 912 and king from 919, the founder of the Saxon (Ottonian) dynasty.
In 926 he won a nine-year truce from the Magyars in return for a captured chieftain and yearly tribute.
He used the respite to build fortresses and train heavy cavalry.
In 933 he defeated the Magyars at Riade; he died in 936.
RULER_KAR_OTTO_I: Otto I the Great, King of Germany (Emperor from 962)
RULER_KAR_OTTO_I_BIO:
Son of Henry the Fowler, crowned king at Aachen in 936.
In his early decades he had to crush rebel dukes, among them his own brothers and his son.
In 955 he routed the Magyars on the Lechfeld; their leaders Bulcsú and Lél were hanged at Regensburg.
Crowned emperor in Rome in 962, he died in 973 and was buried at Magdeburg.
RULER_KAR_OTTO_II_BIO:
Son of Otto the Great, crowned co-emperor in 967 and sole ruler from 973.
In 972 he married the Byzantine princess Theophanu, a great gain in prestige for the dynasty.
In 982 he suffered a heavy defeat against the Saracens at Capo Colonna in Calabria.
He died suddenly in Rome in 983, the only German emperor buried at St Peter's.
RULER_KAR_OTTO_III: Otto III, King of Germany (Emperor from 996)
RULER_KAR_OTTO_III_BIO:
Son of Otto II, king at the age of three in 983; his mother Theophanu, then grandmother Adelaide, ruled.
Crowned emperor in 996, he dreamed of a renewal of the Roman Empire (renovatio imperii).
In 1000 he went on pilgrimage to Gniezno and, by tradition, assented to the crowning of Stephen of Hungary.
He died childless in Italy in 1002, aged just 21.
RULER_KAR_HENRY_II: Henry II, King of Germany (Emperor from 1014)
RULER_KAR_HENRY_II_BIO:
Duke of Bavaria and last of the Ottonians, king from 1002 and crowned emperor in 1014.
His sister Gisela was the wife of King Stephen I of Hungary, so relations with Hungary were good.
In 1007 he founded the bishopric of Bamberg; he fought long wars against Bolesław the Brave of Poland.
He died childless in 1024 and was canonised in 1146.
RULER_KAR_CONRAD_II: Conrad II, King of Germany (Emperor from 1027)
RULER_KAR_CONRAD_II_BIO:
Elected king in 1024, he founded the Salian imperial dynasty.
Crowned emperor in Rome in 1027, he also acquired the Kingdom of Burgundy in 1033.
His 1030 campaign against Hungary failed, and Stephen's army pushed as far as Vienna.
He made peace with Stephen in 1031 and died at Utrecht in 1039.
RULER_KAR_HENRY_III: Henry III, King of Germany (Emperor from 1046)
RULER_KAR_HENRY_III_BIO:
Son of Conrad II, king from 1039; in 1046 he settled the papal schism at Sutri and was crowned emperor.
In 1044 he defeated Samuel Aba at Ménfő and restored Peter Orseolo to the Hungarian throne.
In 1045 Peter did homage to him for Hungary, but this dependence did not last.
His campaigns of 1051 and 1052 against Andrew I failed; he died in 1056.
RULER_KAR_HENRY_IV: Henry IV, King of Germany (Emperor from 1084)
RULER_KAR_HENRY_IV_BIO:
Son of Henry III, king at six in 1056; his mother Agnes ruled during his minority.
In 1063 he restored his brother-in-law Solomon, husband of his sister Judith, to the Hungarian throne.
His investiture struggle with Pope Gregory VII led to his penance at Canossa in 1077.
Crowned emperor by his antipope in 1084, he faced rebellions, later including his own sons.
RULER_NEU_COUNTS: the Frankish counts of the Seine lands
RULER_NEU_COUNTS_BIO:
Under Charlemagne the districts of Rouen, Évreux and Bayeux were run by counts appointed by the emperor.
Royal envoys, the missi dominici, supervised their work.
The coast was still quiet in the early 800s, though Charlemagne already organised coastal defences.
In 841 Vikings burned Rouen, and from then on they sailed up the Seine regularly.
RULER_NEU_ROBERT_STRONG: Robert the Strong, Margrave of Neustria
RULER_NEU_ROBERT_STRONG_BIO:
A Frankish noble whom Charles the Bald made commander of the march between Seine and Loire around 861.
For years he fought the Vikings of the Loire and the Seine as well as the Bretons.
He fell in 866 at Brissarthe, fighting a Viking band under Hastein and its Breton allies.
His sons Odo and Robert later became kings; the Capetian dynasty descends from him.
RULER_NEU_HUGH_ABBOT: Hugh the Abbot, lord of Neustria
RULER_NEU_HUGH_ABBOT_BIO:
A Welf lay abbot and cousin of Charles the Bald, he held several wealthy abbeys.
After Robert the Strong fell in 866, he received Neustria and the guardianship of Robert's sons.
As chief counsellor of Louis the Stammerer and his sons, he held West Francia together for years.
He fought the Vikings often and died in 886, during the siege of Paris.
RULER_SAX_WIDUKIND_BIO:
A Westphalian noble, the best-known leader of Saxon resistance to Charlemagne.
In 777 he stayed away from the assembly at Paderborn and fled to the king of the Danes.
In 782 he routed a Frankish army at the Süntel hills, which Charlemagne avenged at the massacre of Verden.
In 785 he was baptised at Attigny with Charlemagne as godfather; his later fate is unknown.
RULER_SAX_NOBLES_BIO:
After Widukind's baptism part of the Saxon nobility cooperated with the Franks.
The harsh Saxon Capitulary punished pagan customs and refusal of baptism with death.
From 792 revolts flared up again, especially among the Saxons north of the Elbe.
Charlemagne broke them with mass deportations; the last resistance ended in 804.
RULER_SAX_COUNTS_BIO:
Conquered Saxony was run in the emperor's name by Frankish counts and loyal Saxon nobles.
Bishoprics were founded, among them Paderborn, Münster, Osnabrück and Bremen.
In 841–842 the Stellinga uprising of Saxon freemen and freedmen demanded a return to the old ways.
Louis the German crushed it ruthlessly, and the Saxon nobility merged into the Frankish elite.
RULER_SAX_LIUDOLF: Liudolf, Duke of the Eastern Saxons
RULER_SAX_LIUDOLF_BIO:
A Saxon count whom a contemporary source calls duke (dux) of the eastern Saxons.
Around 852 he and his wife Oda founded the convent of Gandersheim.
His daughter Liutgard married Louis the Younger, king of East Francia, raising the family's standing.
He died in 866; the Liudolfing house of Henry the Fowler and Otto the Great is named after him.
RULER_SAX_BRUNO_BIO:
Eldest son of Liudolf, leader of the Saxons after his father's death in 866.
By tradition he founded the town of Brunswick, though this is uncertain.
He fell in February 880 fighting Danish Vikings on the Lüneburg Heath.
Two bishops and many Saxon counts died with him; his brother Otto took over Saxony.
RULER_SAX_OTTO_ILLUSTRIOUS: Otto the Illustrious, Duke of Saxony
RULER_SAX_OTTO_ILLUSTRIOUS_BIO:
Son of Liudolf, he led the Saxons after his brother Bruno fell in 880.
He was also lay abbot of Hersfeld and on good terms with the Carolingian kings.
Widukind of Corvey claims he was offered the crown in 911 and declined; this is doubtful.
He died in 912; his duchy passed to his son Henry, the future king.
RULER_SAX_HERMANN_BILLUNG_BIO:
In 936 Otto the Great made him military commander (princeps militiae) on the lower Elbe frontier.
For decades he fought the Obodrites and other Elbe Slavs.
He deputised for the king in Saxony during Otto's Italian journeys, founding the Billung ducal house.
In 972 he had himself received like a king at Magdeburg, angering Otto; he died in 973.
RULER_SAX_BERNARD_I_BIO:
Son of Hermann Billung, Duke of Saxony from 973.
In the great Slav uprising of 983 most of the lands beyond the Elbe were lost.
In 984 he backed the child king Otto III against Henry the Quarrelsome's bid for the throne.
He also fought Danish and Slav incursions, and died in 1011.
RULER_SAX_BERNARD_II_BIO:
Son of Bernard I, Duke of Saxony for nearly half a century, from 1011 to 1059.
Early on he rose against Emperor Henry II, but they were reconciled in 1020.
Later he waged a long feud with the powerful Archbishop Adalbert of Bremen.
He held loose overlordship over the Elbe Slavs and died in 1059.
RULER_SAX_ORDULF_BIO:
Son of Bernard II, duke 1059–1072; his wife Wulfhild was a daughter of St Olaf of Norway.
In 1066 a pagan Obodrite revolt killed Prince Gottschalk and swept away Saxon influence.
Ordulf failed to restore Saxon lordship beyond the Elbe.
His son Magnus, the last Billung duke, ruled until 1106 and also rebelled against Henry IV.
RULER_STR_KINGS_BIO:
The British kingdom on the Clyde had its centre on Dumbarton Rock, Alt Clut, the Rock of the Britons.
Its people spoke Cumbric, a language close to Welsh.
Of its 8th- and 9th-century kings we know little more than names, from brief notes in Welsh annals.
The Annales Cambriae record that Alt Clut burned in 780.
RULER_STR_ARTHGAL_BIO:
The start of his reign is unknown; Irish annals mention him only around 870.
In 870 the Viking kings of Dublin, Olaf and Ivar, besieged Dumbarton for four months.
When its well ran dry the fortress fell, and in 871 captives were taken to Dublin in 200 ships.
In 872 he was killed at the instigation of Constantine I, king of the Scots.
RULER_STR_RHUN_BIO:
Son of Arthgal, he became king after his father's murder in 872.
His wife was a daughter of Kenneth mac Alpin, tying him closely to the Scots.
After the fall of Dumbarton the kingdom's centre moved up the Clyde, around Govan.
From now on it is known as Strathclyde (Ystrad Clud) rather than Alt Clut.
RULER_STR_EOCHAID_BIO:
Son of Rhun and grandson of Kenneth mac Alpin, which gave him a claim to the Scottish throne.
Some later chronicles say that after 878 he ruled over the Scots together with Giric.
The sources are confused; it is unclear whether he truly reigned or was Giric's puppet.
Around 889 he was driven out along with Giric; his later fate is unknown.
RULER_STR_DYFNWAL_BIO:
A Scottish chronicle names him king of the Britons, a contemporary of Constantine II of the Scots.
His origins are uncertain; some historians think he was related to the Scottish royal house.
In his time the kingdom probably expanded south into what is now Cumbria.
The chronicle places his death between 908 and 915.
RULER_STR_OWAIN: Owain ap Dyfnwal, King of Strathclyde
RULER_STR_OWAIN_BIO:
Son of Dyfnwal, king of the Cumbrians; by some accounts he submitted to Æthelstan at Eamont in 927.
He allied with Constantine II of the Scots and Olaf Guthfrithson of Dublin against the English.
In 937 he fought at Brunanburh, where the allies suffered a crushing defeat.
Some historians think he fell in the battle, but this is uncertain.
RULER_STR_DYFNWAL_III: Dyfnwal ab Owain, King of Strathclyde
RULER_STR_DYFNWAL_III_BIO:
Son of Owain, he took over after Brunanburh and reigned for almost four decades.
In 945 King Edmund of England ravaged Cumbria and granted it to Malcolm I of the Scots.
A later chronicle claims that Edmund had two of Dyfnwal's sons blinded.
In old age he probably abdicated, and he died on pilgrimage to Rome in 975.
RULER_STR_MAEL_COLUIM_BIO:
Son of Dyfnwal, he became king around 975, when his father left on pilgrimage.
By tradition he was at Chester in 973, where several kings submitted to Edgar of England.
Little is known of his reign; his realm balanced between the Scots and the English.
According to Irish annals he died in 997.
RULER_STR_OWAIN_BALD: Owain the Bald, King of Strathclyde
RULER_STR_OWAIN_BALD_BIO:
The last known king of Strathclyde; his parentage and accession are uncertain.
After Máel Coluim there were probably other short reigns; the sources are thin here.
In 1018 he fought beside Malcolm II of Scotland and defeated the Northumbrians at Carham.
He probably died soon after the battle, and the kingdom passed under Scottish control.
RULER_STR_SCOTS_BIO:
After 1018 Strathclyde, or Cumbria, came under the rule of the kings of Scots.
By tradition Duncan I was king of the Cumbrians before he took the Scottish throne.
Its southern part, around Carlisle, stayed contested between Scots and English.
In 1092 William II of England seized Carlisle and built a castle there.
RULER_BRE_MACHTIERNS: the Breton machtierns and petty lords
RULER_BRE_MACHTIERNS_BIO:
Machtierns were Breton local lords, each heading a rural community (plebs).
There was no united Breton power yet, and the petty lords often feuded among themselves.
The Franks tried to impose their lordship from the Breton March, their frontier zone.
Frankish campaigns in 786 and 799 forced submission, but only for a time.
RULER_BRE_MORVAN_BIO:
A Breton lord who took the title of king and refused tribute and fealty to Louis the Pious.
In the poem of Ermoldus Nigellus he proudly rejects the emperor's envoy.
In 818 Louis marched into Brittany with a great army, and Morvan was killed in the fighting.
After his death the Bretons submitted to the Franks for a time.
RULER_BRE_WIOMARCH_BIO:
A Breton lord who rose against Frankish rule in 822.
In 824 Louis the Pious led a campaign against him in person and ravaged Brittany.
In 825 Wiomarch submitted to the emperor at Aachen and was pardoned.
After returning home, however, he was killed by the men of Count Lambert of Nantes.
RULER_BRE_NOMINOE_BIO:
Count of Vannes, whom Louis the Pious made imperial envoy (missus) over the Bretons in 831.
After Louis died he turned against Charles the Bald and defeated him at Ballon in 845.
In 848–849 he deposed pro-Frankish bishops and sought to make Dol a Breton archbishopric.
He died on campaign in Frankish lands in 851; later tradition calls him father of the Breton nation.
RULER_BRE_ERISPOE_BIO:
Son of Nominoe, he won a decisive victory over Charles the Bald at Jengland in August 851.
At the peace of Angers Charles recognised his royal title and ceded Rennes, Nantes and Retz.
He betrothed his daughter to Charles's son Louis the Stammerer, a sign of rapprochement.
In 857 his cousin Salomon's men murdered him at a church altar.
RULER_BRE_SALOMON_BIO:
Cousin and murderer of Erispoe, he ruled from 857; under him Brittany reached its greatest extent.
Charles the Bald ceded him part of Anjou in 863 and the Cotentin and Avranchin in 867.
He both allied with and fought the Vikings; in 866 he fought at Brissarthe alongside Hastein.
In 874 his nobles conspired and killed him; he was later venerated as a saint.
RULER_BRE_ALAN_GREAT: Alan the Great, King of the Bretons
RULER_BRE_ALAN_GREAT_BIO:
Count of Vannes; after Salomon's murder the Breton lords fought a civil war for years.
After 877 he shared power with his rival Judicael until Judicael fell fighting the Vikings.
Around 890 he won a crushing victory over the Vikings at Questembert.
He then ruled alone and is called king in the sources; he died in 907.
RULER_BRE_NORSE_BIO:
After Alan the Great's death Vikings ravaged Brittany almost unopposed.
In 913 they sacked the abbey of Landévennec, and the monks fled with their relics.
In 919 Rögnvald's Vikings occupied the land, and Breton lords fled to Francia and England.
A Breton revolt in 931 was crushed; Nantes became a Viking base.
RULER_BRE_ALAN_BARBETORTE_BIO:
Grandson of Alan the Great, he fled as a child to the court of King Æthelstan of England.
He returned in 936 with English backing and drove the Vikings out of Nantes in 937.
His decisive victory at Trans in 939 ended Viking rule in Brittany.
He made Nantes his seat and rebuilt it; he died in 952.
RULER_BRE_CONAN_I_BIO:
Count of Rennes, he fought for decades against Barbetorte's heirs and the counts of Nantes.
In 990 he seized Nantes and took the title of Duke of Brittany.
Fulk Nerra of Anjou attacked him to restore his own influence over Nantes.
In 992 he was killed fighting Fulk at the battle of Conquereuil.
RULER_BRE_GEOFFREY_I_BIO:
Son of Conan I, Duke of Brittany from 992.
He sealed an alliance with Duke Richard II of Normandy: each married the other's sister.
Few details of his reign survive; Rennes was the centre of his power.
He died on pilgrimage in 1008; legend says a woman stoned him after his hawk attacked her hen.
RULER_BRE_ALAN_III_BIO:
Son of Geoffrey I, duke as a child under the guardianship of his mother Hawise and Richard II of Normandy.
As a young man he crushed a Breton peasant revolt and fought both Anjou and Normandy.
From 1035 he was a guardian of the boy William of Normandy, the future Conqueror.
He died suddenly in Normandy in 1040; some sources say he was poisoned.
RULER_BRE_CONAN_II_BIO:
Son of Alan III, duke as a small child; his uncle Eudes governed in his place.
In 1057 he seized real power and imprisoned his uncle.
In 1064 Duke William of Normandy campaigned against him, as shown on the Bayeux Tapestry.
He died in 1066 while campaigning against Anjou; Breton tradition says he was poisoned.
RULER_BRE_HOEL_II_BIO:
Count of Cornouaille, he married Conan II's sister Hawise and so became duke in 1066.
That same year many Breton knights fought for William the Conqueror at Hastings.
His reign was marked by revolts of Breton lords and tense relations with Normandy.
He died in 1084; his son Alan IV Fergant ruled Brittany until 1112.
RULER_WSL_WITZAN_BIO:
Prince of the Obotrite Slavs on the lower Elbe in the late 8th century.
A loyal ally of Charlemagne in his long wars against the Saxons.
In 789 he marched with the Franks against the Veleti (Wilzi).
In 795 Saxons ambushed and killed him while he was crossing the Elbe.
RULER_WSL_THRASCO_BIO:
Witzan's successor as prince of the Obotrites and a faithful ally of Charlemagne.
In 798 he crushed the Nordalbingian Saxons at Sventana near Bornhöved.
In 808 the Danish king Godfred invaded and destroyed the trading town of Reric.
He was murdered by Godfred's men in 809.
RULER_WSL_SLAOMIR_BIO:
Became ruler of the Obotrites with Frankish approval after Thrasco's death.
In 817 he rebelled when ordered to share power with Ceadrag.
He allied with the Danes against the Franks but was captured in 818.
Deposed and exiled in 819, he was baptised shortly before his death.
RULER_WSL_CEADRAG_BIO:
Son of Thrasco, sole ruler of the Obotrites from 819 after Slaomir's fall.
He too was soon accused of disloyalty at the Frankish court.
He kept ties with the Danes while Louis the Pious demanded his obedience.
The sources last mention him around 826; his later fate is unknown.
RULER_WSL_GOSTOMYSL_BIO:
Obotrite king recorded as Gestimus or Gostomuizli in the Frankish annals.
He fell in 844 when Louis the German campaigned against the Obotrites.
After his death the Franks divided his realm among several lesser princes.
Not the legendary Gostomysl of Novgorod; beyond his death little is known.
RULER_WSL_NAKON_BIO:
Founder of the Nakonid dynasty of the Obotrites in the mid-10th century.
In 955 Otto I defeated his brother Stoignew on the Recknitz river.
Nakon survived the disaster and seems to have ruled until about 965.
The Jewish traveller Ibrahim ibn Yaqub names him among the great Slav rulers.
RULER_WSL_MIESZKO_I_BIO:
First historically known Piast ruler of the Polans, from about 960.
Baptised in 966, encouraged by his Bohemian wife Dobrawa.
In 972 he defeated Margrave Hodo at the battle of Cedynia.
Around 991 the Dagome iudex document placed his lands under papal protection.
RULER_WSL_BOLESLAW_I_BIO:
Son of Mieszko I, duke of Poland from 992.
At the Congress of Gniezno in 1000 Emperor Otto III hailed him as a friend.
He entered Kyiv in 1018 and fought long wars with Emperor Henry II.
He was crowned the first King of Poland in 1025, shortly before his death.
RULER_WSL_MIESZKO_II_BIO:
Son of Bolesław the Brave, crowned King of Poland in 1025.
A learned ruler who reportedly knew Latin and Greek.
In 1031 a German and Kyivan attack forced him to flee to Bohemia.
He returned only by giving up the royal title and died in 1034 amid chaos.
RULER_WSL_CASIMIR_I_BIO:
Son of Mieszko II, driven out of Poland during the unrest of the 1030s.
In his absence a pagan revolt and a Bohemian invasion devastated the land.
Returning around 1039 with German and Kyivan help, he rebuilt the state.
He made Kraków his seat and died in 1058.
RULER_WSL_BOLESLAW_II_BIO:
Son of Casimir the Restorer, duke of Poland from 1058.
He sided with Pope Gregory VII against Emperor Henry IV.
Crowned king in 1076, he also meddled in Hungary's succession struggles.
After having Bishop Stanislaus of Kraków killed in 1079, he fled to Hungary.
RULER_WSL_WLADYSLAW_HERMAN_BIO:
Younger brother of Bolesław the Bold, duke of Poland from 1079.
He did not take the royal title and sought peace with the Empire.
For years real power lay with his hated palatine Sieciech.
His sons Zbigniew and Bolesław III divided the land while he still lived.
RULER_MOR_CHIEFS_BIO:
Leaders of the Slavic tribes along the Morava river in the late 8th century.
They ruled from fortified strongholds such as Mikulčice and Staré Město.
The fall of the Avar Khaganate freed them from their eastern neighbour.
They drew ever closer to the Franks and to Christian missionaries.
RULER_MOR_MOJMIR_I_BIO:
First known ruler of the Mojmírid dynasty and founder of Great Moravia.
Around 833 he drove Pribina out of Nitra and united the Moravians.
Under his rule missionaries from Passau baptised many Moravians.
In 846 Louis the German deposed him and installed his nephew Rastislav.
RULER_MOR_RASTISLAV_BIO:
Nephew of Mojmír I, placed on the Moravian throne by Louis the German in 846.
He soon turned against the Franks and defended his realm successfully.
In 862 he asked Emperor Michael III for missionaries speaking Slavonic.
Cyril and Methodius came in 863; in 870 Svatopluk betrayed him to the Franks.
RULER_MOR_SVATOPLUK_BIO:
Nephew of Rastislav, ruler of Great Moravia from 871.
Under him the realm reached from Bohemia to the Vistula and the Tisza.
He backed Archbishop Methodius, though later he favoured the Latin clergy.
Hungarian legend says the Magyars bought his land for a white horse; he died in 894.
RULER_MOR_MOJMIR_II_BIO:
Son of Svatopluk I, from 894 the last known ruler of Great Moravia.
He fought a civil war against his brother Svatopluk II of Nitra.
Around 899–900 the pope sent him a new archbishop and bishops.
He vanishes from the sources around 906 as Magyar attacks broke his realm.
RULER_MOR_SPYTIHNEV_I_BIO:
Son of Bořivoj, the first Přemyslid duke as Great Moravia declined.
In 895 he led the Bohemian dukes to submit to East Francia at Regensburg.
This broke Moravian overlordship and tied Bohemia to the Latin Church.
He fortified Prague Castle and Budeč; he died around 915.
RULER_MOR_VRATISLAUS_I_BIO:
Younger brother of Spytihněv, duke of Bohemia from 915.
His wife was Drahomíra, a pagan-born princess of the Hevelli.
He founded the Basilica of St George at Prague Castle.
He died in 921, by some accounts fighting the Magyars.
RULER_MOR_WENCESLAS_BIO:
Son of Vratislaus I, raised as a Christian by his grandmother Saint Ludmila.
During his minority his mother Drahomíra ruled and Ludmila was murdered.
As duke he paid tribute to King Henry I of Germany.
His brother Boleslaus killed him in 935; he became Bohemia's patron saint.
RULER_MOR_BOLESLAUS_I_BIO:
Brother of Saint Wenceslas, who seized the throne by killing him in 935.
He fought Otto I for fourteen years before accepting his overlordship in 950.
In 955 his troops fought the Magyars at the Lechfeld.
He ruled Silesia and Kraków; his daughter Dobrawa married Mieszko I.
RULER_MOR_BOLESLAUS_II_BIO:
Son of Boleslaus I, duke of Bohemia from 972.
Under him the bishopric of Prague was founded around 973.
In 995 he had the rival Slavník clan massacred at Libice.
He lost Silesia and Kraków to the Poles late in life and died in 999.
RULER_MOR_BOLESLAUS_III_BIO:
Son of Boleslaus II, duke of Bohemia from 999, notorious for his cruelty.
Expelled in 1002, he briefly returned with Polish help.
In 1003 Bolesław the Brave had him blinded and seized Prague.
He spent the rest of his life in Polish captivity and died in 1037.
RULER_MOR_OLDRICH_BIO:
Son of Boleslaus II, who became duke in 1012 by ousting his brother Jaromír.
He won Moravia back from the Poles and gave it to his son Bretislav.
By tradition he married the peasant girl Božena, Bretislav's mother.
In 1034 he had Jaromír blinded and died later that same year.
RULER_MOR_BRETISLAV_I_BIO:
Son of Oldřich, duke of Bohemia from 1035, called the Bohemian Achilles.
He carried off his wife Judith of Schweinfurt from a convent.
In 1039 he raided Poland and took the relics of Saint Adalbert from Gniezno.
Defeated by Henry III in 1041, he set up the rule of seniority for succession.
RULER_MOR_SPYTIHNEV_II_BIO:
Eldest son of Bretislav I, duke of Bohemia from 1055.
At his accession he expelled the Germans, his own mother among them.
He kept his younger brothers in Moravia under tight control.
He began rebuilding the St Vitus rotunda in Prague as a basilica; died 1061.
RULER_MOR_VRATISLAUS_II_BIO:
Son of Bretislav I, duke of Bohemia from 1061.
His second wife was Adelaide, daughter of King Andrew I of Hungary.
He was a loyal ally of Emperor Henry IV in the Investiture Controversy.
As reward he became Bohemia's first king in 1085, a title for his lifetime only.
RULER_AVA_KHAGAN_BIO:
Supreme ruler of the Avar Khaganate; his personal name is not recorded.
His seat was the Ring, a fortified camp famed for its treasure.
From 791 Charlemagne's armies struck ever deeper into his realm.
In 795 he and the jugurrus were killed in civil strife; the Franks looted the Ring.
RULER_AVA_TUDUN_BIO:
One of the highest Avar dignitaries; his personal name is not recorded.
In 795 he sent envoys to Charlemagne and offered his submission.
In 796 he came to Aachen and was baptised with his followers.
He soon broke faith and, the annals say, paid for his treachery.
RULER_AVA_THEODORE_BIO:
A Christian Avar kapkhan after the fall of the Khaganate.
In 805 he travelled to Aachen because the Slavs were pressing his people.
Charlemagne granted them land between Savaria and Carnuntum.
He died soon after his return; the khagan who followed was also baptised.
RULER_AVA_CHIEFS_BIO:
Leaders of the Avar remnant under Frankish overlordship.
In 811 the Franks had to settle feuds between Avars and Slavs.
Avar envoys appeared at the Frankish court for the last time in 822.
Their people then slowly merged into the Slavs and the Frankish marches.
RULER_MAG_CHIEFS_BIO:
Leaders of the seven Magyar tribes on the steppe, in Levedia and Etelköz.
They lived as allies of the Khazar Khaganate, partly under its sway.
They were mounted nomads, though they also practised farming.
They were joined by the Kabars, rebels who had broken with the Khazars.
RULER_MAG_LEVEDI_BIO:
According to Constantine Porphyrogenitus, the first voivode of the Magyars.
The Magyar homeland of Levedia was named after him.
The Khazar khagan gave him a noble Khazar woman as wife.
He declined supreme rule and put forward Álmos or Árpád instead.
RULER_MAG_ALMOS_BIO:
Son of Ügyek and Emese; legend says the turul bird foretold his birth.
By the chronicles, the seven chiefs chose him as prince by a blood oath.
He led his people from Etelköz towards the Carpathians.
A chronicle says he was killed in Transylvania before the conquest was done.
RULER_MAG_ARPAD_BIO:
Son of Álmos, prince of the conquering Magyars and founder of the Árpád dynasty.
Around 895 he led his people into the Carpathian Basin.
The Magyars took the Great Plain and Pannonia and broke Great Moravia.
He died around 907, the year the Bavarian army was crushed at Pressburg.
RULER_MAG_ZOLTA_BIO:
According to the Anonymous Notary, Árpád's youngest son and successor.
In his time Magyar raiders rode from Italy to Saxony and Burgundy.
In 933 Henry I defeated a Magyar army near Merseburg.
His real role is uncertain; the raids were led by chiefs such as Bulcsú.
RULER_MAG_FAJSZ_BIO:
Grandson of Árpád, named as prince only by Constantine Porphyrogenitus.
He ruled around 948, when Bulcsú and Termacsu visited Constantinople.
There Bulcsú was baptised and given a Byzantine court title.
The Hungarian chronicles do not know him; the extent of his power is unclear.
RULER_MAG_TAKSONY_BIO:
Son of Zolta, who by the chronicles became prince after the Lechfeld defeat.
After 955 the raids to the West ended, though raids to the south went on.
He settled Pechenegs and Muslim Ishmaelites in the country.
Sources say he asked Rome for a bishop around 963; he died around 972.
RULER_MAG_GEZA_BIO:
Son of Taksony, prince of the Magyars from about 972.
In 973 he sent envoys to Otto I at Quedlinburg and made peace.
He invited Western missionaries and was baptised himself.
He ruled with an iron hand; his son Vajk (Stephen) married a Bavarian princess.
RULER_MAG_STEPHEN_I_BIO:
Son of Géza, prince from 997; he defeated his rival Koppány.
He was crowned King of Hungary at Christmas 1000 or early in 1001.
He organised the counties and the Church, headed by the see of Esztergom.
His son Emeric died in 1031; Stephen was canonised in 1083.
RULER_MAG_PETER_BIO:
Venetian son of Stephen's sister, named heir by the king; he reigned from 1038.
Favouring foreigners, he was driven out in 1041 and Samuel Aba took the throne.
In 1044 Henry III restored him after the battle of Ménfő; he became his vassal.
In 1046 he was captured and blinded during the pagan revolt of Vata.
RULER_MAG_SAMUEL_ABA_BIO:
Brother-in-law of King Stephen, from a clan said to be of Kabar origin.
He was elected king in 1041 after Peter Orseolo was driven out.
He raided the Empire but lost the support of many of his nobles.
Henry III defeated him at Ménfő in 1044; he was killed while fleeing.
RULER_MAG_ANDREW_I_BIO:
Son of Vazul, who returned from Kyivan Rus and took the throne in 1046.
His wife Anastasia was a daughter of Yaroslav the Wise of Kyiv.
In 1051 and 1052 he beat back the invasions of Henry III.
He fell out with his brother Béla over the succession and died in 1060.
RULER_MAG_BELA_I_BIO:
Andrew's brother, who defeated him with Polish help and became king in 1060.
He had spent years in Poland and married into the Piast dynasty.
In 1061 he crushed the last great pagan revolt and reformed the coinage.
In 1063 his throne collapsed on him at Dömös and he died of his injuries.
RULER_MAG_SOLOMON_BIO:
Son of Andrew I, crowned as a child in 1057, he took the throne in 1063.
His wife Judith was a sister of Emperor Henry IV.
With his cousins Géza and Ladislaus he beat steppe raiders and took Belgrade.
They fell out, and after his defeat at Mogyoród in 1074 he lost his power.
RULER_MAG_GEZA_I_BIO:
Son of Béla I, who defeated Solomon at Mogyoród in 1074.
Solomon held out in Pressburg, so Géza's rule stayed contested.
Emperor Michael VII sent him a crown, now the lower part of the Holy Crown.
He was negotiating Solomon's abdication when he died in 1077.
RULER_MAG_LADISLAUS_I_BIO:
Son of Béla I, he became king in 1077 after his brother Géza's death.
In 1083 he had Stephen, Emeric and Gerard canonised.
He restored order with harsh laws and founded the bishopric of Várad.
In 1091 he occupied Croatia; the knight-king was canonised in 1192.
RULER_PEC_CHIEFS_BIO:
Leaders of the Turkic-speaking Pecheneg tribes beyond the Volga.
Constantine Porphyrogenitus counts eight tribes under elected chiefs.
Around 893, pressed by the Oghuz and Khazars, they moved west.
In Etelköz they attacked the Magyars and seized their pastures.
RULER_PEC_KURYA_BIO:
A Pecheneg khan of the later 10th century.
In 968 the Pechenegs laid siege to Kyiv.
In 972 he ambushed and killed Prince Sviatoslav of Kyiv at the Dnieper rapids.
The Primary Chronicle says he made a gilded drinking cup of his skull.
RULER_PEC_TYRACH_BIO:
Son of Kilder, a Pecheneg khan of noble lineage.
In 1036 Yaroslav the Wise dealt the Pechenegs a crushing defeat at Kyiv.
He was the bitter rival of Kegen, a chief of humble birth.
In late 1048 he crossed the Danube with a vast host but Byzantium defeated him.
RULER_PEC_KEGEN_BIO:
A Pecheneg leader of humble birth who rose through his deeds in war.
Beaten by Tyrach, he fled with his followers to Byzantium.
He was baptised, made a patrikios and given forts on the Danube.
From there he raided the Pechenegs across the river; he was murdered around 1050.
RULER_SSL_VISESLAV_BIO:
Duke of the Dalmatian Croats around 800, the first Croatian ruler known by name.
His name survives on the baptismal font from Nin.
In his time Christianity spread among the Croats.
Little else is known; he is not the Serbian prince of the same name.
RULER_SSL_BORNA_BIO:
Duke of the Dalmatian Croats from about 810, under Frankish overlordship.
Frankish annals also call him duke of the Guduscani.
In 819 he fought for the Franks against the revolt of Ljudevit of Pannonia.
Some of his men deserted him, but he held on to power; he died in 821.
RULER_SSL_VLADISLAV_BIO:
Nephew of Borna, chosen in 821 by the people with the emperor's consent.
He ruled Dalmatian Croatia as a vassal of the Franks.
In his time the Franks put down Ljudevit's revolt.
Little is known of his reign; Mislav followed him around 835.
RULER_SSL_MISLAV_BIO:
Croatian duke from around 835, with his seat near Klis.
In 839 he made peace with the Venetian doge Pietro Tradonico.
In his time Croatian sea power became a growing worry for Venice.
He built a church at Putalj; Trpimir succeeded him around 845.
RULER_SSL_TRPIMIR_BIO:
Founder of the Trpimirović dynasty, duke of the Croats from around 845.
His charter of 852 calls him dux Chroatorum, duke of the Croats.
He fought Byzantines and Bulgars; the monk Gottschalk visited his court.
He founded the first Benedictine house in Croatia at Rižinice; died c. 864.
RULER_SSL_DOMAGOJ_BIO:
He seized power from the sons of Trpimir in 864.
His fleet threatened Venice and Adriatic shipping for years.
In 871 he helped besiege Arab-held Bari.
Venetian writers called him the worst duke of the Slavs; he died in 876.
RULER_SSL_BRANIMIR_BIO:
In 879 he overthrew the pro-Byzantine duke Zdeslav.
That same year Pope John VIII blessed him and his people.
This papal blessing is seen as the first recognition of a Croatian state.
Inscriptions call him dux Cruatorum; he died around 892.
RULER_SSL_MUNCIMIR_BIO:
Son of Trpimir, who won back the throne for his family around 892.
His charter of 892 styles him duke of the Croats by the grace of God.
In it he settled a dispute between the churches of Nin and Split.
His reign was largely peaceful; he died around 910.
RULER_SSL_TOMISLAV_BIO:
Duke of the Croats from about 910 and, by tradition, first king from 925.
A letter of Pope John X in 925 addresses him as rex, king.
By tradition he repelled the Magyars and united Pannonian and Dalmatian Croats.
In 926 he crushed the army of Tsar Simeon of Bulgaria.
RULER_SSL_CASLAV_BIO:
Serbian prince of the Vlastimirović line, back from Bulgarian captivity c. 927.
After Tsar Simeon's death he rebuilt ravaged Serbia.
He ruled as a client of Byzantium, with its support.
By tradition he died fighting the Magyars, drowned in the Sava.
RULER_SSL_STJEPAN_DRZISLAV_BIO:
He took the Croatian throne around 969 and steadied the realm after civil strife.
Thomas the Archdeacon says he received royal insignia from Byzantium.
He was an ally of Byzantium against Tsar Samuel of Bulgaria.
He died in 997; his sons' quarrels over the throne weakened the kingdom.
RULER_SSL_KRESIMIR_III_BIO:
Son of Stjepan Držislav, ruling from about 1000 jointly with his brother Gojslav.
In 1000 the Venetian doge Pietro II Orseolo seized the Dalmatian towns.
He tried to win them back, but Venice's pact with Byzantium blocked him.
He died around 1030; his son Stephen I married an Orseolo daughter.
RULER_SSL_PETAR_KRESIMIR_IV_BIO:
King of Croatia from 1058, ruling at the height of medieval Croatian power.
He brought the Dalmatian towns and islands under his rule.
In one charter he speaks of our Dalmatian sea.
Around 1074 a Norman count captured him; he died soon afterwards.
RULER_SSL_ZVONIMIR_BIO:
Once ban of Slavonia, crowned king at Solin in 1075 by a legate of Gregory VII.
His wife Helen was a daughter of Béla I and sister of Saint Ladislaus.
He ruled as a papal vassal; the Baška tablet preserves his name.
He died without an heir in 1089, which led Ladislaus to enter Croatia in 1091.
RULER_FIN_ELDERS: the elders of the Finnish tribes
RULER_FIN_ELDERS_BIO:
Leaders of the Finnic communities of Finland Proper, Häme and Karelia.
They had no kings; elders of kin groups and villages settled common affairs.
They traded furs, iron and crafts with the Vikings and the Rus.
Karelia lay on the busy trade routes around Lake Ladoga.
RULER_SAM_ELDERS: the Sámi siida elders and noaidi
RULER_SAM_ELDERS_BIO:
The Sámi had no rulers; elders led the siida, their hunting and fishing bands.
The noaidi, their shamans, used their drums to reach the spirit world.
They moved with the seasons, following reindeer and fishing grounds.
In the 9th century the Norwegian Ohthere took tribute from them in furs and down.
RULER_DOR_ELDERS: the elders of the Dorset (Tuniit) people
RULER_DOR_ELDERS_BIO:
Leaders of the Late Dorset people of Greenland and Arctic Canada.
They lived in small bands hunting seal and walrus, without bow or drill.
They were masterful carvers of bone and ivory, making striking amulets.
Inuit tradition calls them Tuniit; after 1000 the Thule people displaced them.
RULER_DBU_KARDAM_BIO:
Khan of Bulgaria from about 777; neither the start nor the end of his reign is known precisely.
He restored order to a khanate weakened by years of throne struggles.
In 792 he crushed Emperor Constantine VI at Marcellae.
He demanded tribute from Byzantium; he probably died around 803 and was followed by Krum.
RULER_DBU_KRUM_BIO:
Khan of Bulgaria c. 803–814 and one of its greatest conquerors.
After the fall of the Avars he reportedly extended his rule as far as the Tisza.
In 811 he trapped and killed Emperor Nikephoros I and had his skull made into a drinking cup.
In 813 he marched on Constantinople but died in 814 while preparing the assault.
RULER_DBU_OMURTAG_BIO:
Son of Krum, he ruled Bulgaria from 814 to 831.
Around 815 he made a thirty-year peace with Byzantium and fortified the southern border.
He built palaces at Pliska; his Greek-language inscriptions record his deeds.
He persecuted Christians and fought the Franks along the Drava.
RULER_DBU_MALAMIR_BIO:
Omurtag's youngest son, he ruled from 831 to 836.
Much of the government lay with Isbul, the powerful kavkhan.
He had his elder brother Enravota executed for converting to Christianity.
War with Byzantium resumed in 836; some scholars identify him with Presian.
RULER_DBU_PRESIAN_BIO:
Ruler of Bulgaria 836–852; his origins and identity are debated.
Under him Bulgarian power spread over much of Macedonia.
His war against the Serbs in 839–842 ended in failure.
The sources name him as the father of Boris I.
RULER_DBU_BORIS_I_BIO:
Ruler of Bulgaria from 852 to 889.
Baptised around 864 as Michael, he brought his people into the Christian faith.
He bargained between Rome and Constantinople, choosing the Byzantine church in 870.
He welcomed the disciples of Methodius; he became a monk in 889 and is venerated as a saint.
RULER_DBU_VLADIMIR_BIO:
Eldest son of Boris I, he succeeded his father in 889.
According to the sources he tried to restore the old pagan faith.
In 893 his father left the monastery, deposed him and had him blinded.
His brother Simeon took the throne, and Slavonic became the language of the church.
RULER_DBU_SIMEON_BIO:
Son of Boris I, educated in Constantinople; ruled 893–927 and patronised Slavonic letters.
In 894–896 Byzantium set the Magyars on him, and he turned the Pechenegs against them.
That Pecheneg attack helped drive the Magyars into the Carpathian Basin.
In 917 he routed the Byzantines at the Achelous and took the title of tsar.
RULER_DBU_PETER_I_BIO:
Son of Simeon, he reigned from 927 to 969.
He made peace with Byzantium, married Maria Lekapene and had his title of tsar recognised.
His reign saw the rise of the Bogomil heresy and repeated Magyar raids through his lands.
After Sviatoslav of Kiev invaded in 968, he died as a monk in 969.
RULER_DBU_BORIS_II_BIO:
Son of Peter I, he took the throne in 969 with Sviatoslav's army already in the country.
Held by the Rus', he fell into Byzantine hands when John Tzimiskes took Preslav in 971.
In Constantinople he was publicly stripped of his regalia; eastern Bulgaria became Byzantine.
He escaped in 977 but was killed by mistake by a Bulgarian guard at the border.
RULER_DBU_SAMUEL_BIO:
One of the Cometopuli brothers; ruler of western Bulgaria from 977 and tsar from 997.
In 986 he defeated Basil II at Trajan's Gate and extended his rule over much of the Balkans.
He ruled from Ohrid and Prespa; his son Gavril Radomir married a Hungarian princess.
Defeated at Kleidion in 1014, he died soon after seeing his blinded soldiers return.
RULER_DBU_GAVRIL_RADOMIR_BIO:
Son of Samuel, he took the throne on his father's death in 1014.
Known as a brave warrior, by tradition he saved his father's life in 997.
His first wife was a Hungarian princess, probably Géza's daughter, whom he later cast out.
In 1015 his cousin Ivan Vladislav murdered him during a hunt.
RULER_DBU_IVAN_VLADISLAV_BIO:
Son of Aaron and nephew of Samuel; Gavril Radomir had saved his life when Aaron was executed.
He seized the throne in 1015 by murdering Radomir.
Amid truces and broken promises he carried on a hopeless war against Basil II.
He fell besieging Dyrrachium in 1018; after his death Bulgaria surrendered.
RULER_DBU_THEME_BIO:
By 1018 Basil II had conquered Bulgaria, which became a Byzantine province (theme).
It was governed from Skopje; the archbishopric of Ohrid kept its autonomy.
Taxes were first paid in kind; the switch to cash sparked Peter Delyan's revolt in 1040.
Pechenegs and Uzes raided across the Danube, and in 1071 King Salomon of Hungary took Belgrade.
RULER_ABB_HARUN_BIO:
Abbasid caliph 786–809, the famous ruler of the Thousand and One Nights.
Baghdad was then one of the largest and richest cities in the world.
He exchanged embassies with Charlemagne and sent him an elephant named Abul-Abbas.
In 806 he invaded Asia Minor and forced Nikephoros I to pay tribute; he died at Tus in 809.
RULER_ABB_AL_AMIN_BIO:
Son of Harun al-Rashid and Zubayda, he took the throne in 809.
By his father's will the eastern provinces were left to his half-brother al-Ma'mun.
When he named his own son heir, civil war broke out between the brothers.
Tahir's army besieged Baghdad in 812–813; al-Amin was captured and killed.
RULER_ABB_AL_MAMUN_BIO:
Son of Harun and victor of the civil war, he reigned from 813 to 833.
He patronised the House of Wisdom in Baghdad, where Greek science was translated into Arabic.
He imposed an inquisition (mihna) to enforce Mu'tazilite doctrine.
He could not crush Babak's revolt in Azerbaijan; he died in 833 on campaign against Byzantium.
RULER_ABB_AL_MUTASIM_BIO:
Son of Harun, he reigned from 833 to 842.
He built a new army of Turkic slave soldiers loyal to him alone.
In 836 he founded a new capital at Samarra; his general al-Afshin crushed Babak in 837.
In 838 he took revenge by destroying Amorium, ancestral city of Emperor Theophilos.
RULER_ABB_AL_WATHIQ_BIO:
Son of al-Mu'tasim, he reigned from 842 to 847.
He kept up the mihna, while the Turkic officers at his court grew ever stronger.
In 845 he held a great prisoner exchange with Byzantium at the river Lamos.
By tradition he sent Sallam the Interpreter to find the wall of Gog and Magog.
RULER_ABB_AL_MUTAWAKKIL_BIO:
Son of al-Mu'tasim, he reigned from 847 to 861.
He ended the mihna and backed the upholders of Sunni tradition.
His general Bugha crushed the Armenian princes in 852–855, carrying many off to Samarra.
His Turkic guards murdered him in 861; a decade of succession strife followed.
RULER_ABB_AL_MUTAMID_BIO:
He reigned from 870 to 892, but real power lay with his brother al-Muwaffaq.
Al-Muwaffaq crushed the Zanj slave revolt in southern Iraq in 883.
The Tulunids in Egypt and the Saffarids in the east became all but independent.
Around 885 he sent a crown to Ashot I Bagratuni, recognising him as king of Armenia.
RULER_ABB_AL_MUTADID_BIO:
Son of al-Muwaffaq, he reigned 892–902 and restored the authority of the caliphs.
He moved the court back to Baghdad and put the treasury in order.
He bound the Tulunids to him by marriage, but the Qarmatian revolt began in his time.
His son al-Muktafi recovered Egypt for the caliphate in 905.
RULER_ABB_AL_MUQTADIR_BIO:
He took the throne aged thirteen in 908; his reign was plagued by court factions and bankruptcy.
In 921 he sent Ibn Fadlan's embassy to the Volga Bulgars, whose account is a key source.
In 930 the Qarmatians sacked Mecca and carried off the Black Stone.
In 932 he fell in battle against his own general, Mu'nis.
RULER_ABB_BUYIDS: the caliphs under the Buyid emirs
RULER_ABB_BUYIDS_BIO:
In 945 the Shi'ite Buyids entered Baghdad and took over real power.
From then on the caliphs were mere religious figureheads; al-Mustakfi was blinded in 946.
Buyid power peaked under Adud al-Dawla, who died in 983.
In the north the Hamdanids fought Byzantium, which retook Cilicia and Antioch.
RULER_ABB_AL_QADIR_BIO:
He reigned for forty years, 991–1031, in the shadow of the Buyid emirs.
In the Baghdad Manifesto of 1011 he denied the Fatimids' descent from the Prophet.
With the so-called Qadiri creed he made himself the champion of Sunni doctrine.
He was on good terms with Sultan Mahmud of Ghazni, who acknowledged his supremacy.
RULER_ABB_AL_QAIM_BIO:
Son of al-Qadir, he reigned from 1031 to 1075.
Against the failing Buyids he turned to the Seljuk Tughril Beg for help.
In 1058 al-Basasiri seized Baghdad in the name of the Fatimid caliph and drove him into exile.
Tughril restored him in 1060; from then on he lived under the protection of the Seljuk sultans.
RULER_ABB_TUGHRIL_BIO:
Grandson of Seljuk and founder of the Great Seljuk Empire.
In 1040 he defeated the Ghaznavids at Dandanaqan and took Khorasan.
In 1055 he entered Baghdad, ended Buyid rule and was recognised by the caliph as sultan.
In 1054 he besieged Manzikert in Armenia; he died childless at Rayy in 1063.
RULER_ABB_ALP_ARSLAN_BIO:
Nephew of Tughril Beg, he reigned from 1063 to 1072.
In 1064 he took Ani, the old Armenian capital, and also invaded Georgia.
In 1071 he defeated and captured Emperor Romanos IV Diogenes at Manzikert.
His vizier was the great Nizam al-Mulk; in 1072 a prisoner stabbed him to death.
RULER_ABB_MALIK_SHAH_BIO:
Son of Alp Arslan, he reigned 1072–1092, the peak of the Great Seljuk Empire.
His vizier Nizam al-Mulk founded madrasas, colleges of learning, across the empire.
With the help of Omar Khayyam a new, highly accurate calendar was introduced.
In 1092 his vizier was murdered and he died weeks later; succession wars followed.
RULER_GEO_LEON_II_BIO:
Scion of the Abkhazian princely house; the sources say his mother was a Khazar princess.
With Khazar help he threw off Byzantine overlordship and took the title King of the Abkhazians.
He united most of western Georgia and, by tradition, moved his seat to Kutaisi.
The dates of his reign are uncertain, spanning the late 8th and early 9th century.
RULER_GEO_ASHOT_I_BIO:
A member of the Bagrationi house, prince of Iberia (Kartli) from 813.
He made his seat in the fortress of Artanuji in Tao-Klarjeti.
Byzantium granted him the title of kouropalates, and he fought the emir of Tbilisi.
He supported the monastic foundations of Grigol Khandzteli; he was murdered around 830.
RULER_GEO_BAGRAT_I_BIO:
Son of Ashot I, ruler of Iberia 830–876, bearing the Byzantine title of kouropalates.
Against the emir of Tbilisi he at times sided with the caliph in Baghdad.
In 853 the caliph's general Bugha burned Tbilisi and executed the rebel emir.
After his death the branches of the Bagrationi house quarrelled over the lead.
RULER_GEO_ADARNASE: Adarnase IV, King of the Iberians
RULER_GEO_ADARNASE_BIO:
In 888 he took the title King of the Iberians, reviving the kingship of Kartli.
In 891 Byzantium also granted him the title of kouropalates.
He vied with the Abkhazian kings and the Armenian Bagratids for control of Kartli.
He died in 923; his descendants went on ruling in Tao-Klarjeti.
RULER_GEO_GEORGE_II_ABKH_BIO:
King of Abkhazia from 922/923 to 957, at the height of the kingdom's power.
He governed Kartli through his son Leon.
He backed missions to convert the Alans and founded the bishopric of Chqondidi.
Under his successors the kingdom gradually weakened.
RULER_GEO_BAGRAT_III_BIO:
Abkhazian through his mother, Bagratid through his father, adopted by David III of Tao.
King of Abkhazia from 978 and of Kartli from 1008, he created a united Georgian kingdom.
Around 1010 he also conquered Kakheti and Hereti.
He built the Bagrati Cathedral in Kutaisi, named after him; he died in 1014.
RULER_GEO_GEORGE_I_BIO:
Son of Bagrat III, he reigned from 1014 to 1027.
A dispute over the inheritance of Tao dragged him into war with Emperor Basil II.
Defeated in 1021–1022, he ceded lands and gave his son Bagrat as a hostage.
In his reign the Svetitskhoveli Cathedral in Mtskheta was rebuilt.
RULER_GEO_BAGRAT_IV_BIO:
Son of George I, he came to the throne as a child in 1027 and reigned until 1072.
He waged a long struggle against the mighty Duke Liparit Baghuashi and his Byzantine backers.
In 1068 the Seljuk sultan Alp Arslan led a devastating campaign into Georgia.
His daughter, Maria of Alania, became the wife of two Byzantine emperors.
RULER_GEO_GEORGE_II_BIO:
Son of Bagrat IV, he reigned from 1072 to 1089.
His reign saw the Great Turkish Invasion, as Seljuk nomads overran the country.
Around 1080 he submitted to Sultan Malik-Shah and paid him tribute.
In 1089, under pressure from the nobles, he abdicated in favour of his son David.
RULER_GEO_DAVID_IV_BIO:
Son of George II, he came to the throne aged sixteen in 1089 and reigned until 1125.
He strengthened royal power and stopped paying tribute to the Seljuks around 1096.
Later he settled Kipchak warriors in Georgia and built a strong standing army.
He won at Didgori in 1121, retook Tbilisi in 1122 and founded the Gelati monastery.
RULER_RST_ABD_AL_WAHHAB_BIO:
Son of the founder of the Rustamid imamate of Tahert, he ruled from about 784 to 823.
Leader of the Ibadi Kharijites, his election triggered the Nukkarite schism.
He besieged Tripoli against the Aghlabids, after which a border was drawn between them.
Tahert (Tiaret) became a hub of trans-Saharan trade and Ibadi learning.
RULER_RST_AFLAH_BIO:
Son of Abd al-Wahhab, he ruled from 823 to about 871, the Rustamids' golden age.
Tahert grew into a rich trading city drawing Persians, Arabs and Christians.
He kept up an alliance with the Umayyads of Córdoba against the Aghlabids.
The sources say he burned al-Abbasiyya, a town the Aghlabids had founded nearby.
RULER_RST_ABU_L_YAQZAN_BIO:
Son of Aflah, he came to power around 874, reportedly after years as a captive in Baghdad.
His reign was burdened by internal strife and tribal rivalries.
By tradition he was driven from Tahert for a time but regained power.
He died in 894; after him the imamate declined rapidly.
RULER_RST_ABU_HATIM_BIO:
Son of Abu l-Yaqzan, he ruled from 894; once driven out, he later returned.
By now the imamate's power barely reached beyond the environs of Tahert.
Around 906 he was murdered by his nephews.
In 909 Fatimid forces took Tahert, ending Rustamid rule.
RULER_RST_AL_MAHDI_BIO:
Founder of the Fatimid Caliphate, who claimed descent from the Prophet's daughter Fatima.
His missionary Abu Abdallah al-Shi'i led the Kutama Berbers to topple Aghlabids and Rustamids in 909.
Proclaimed caliph at Raqqada in 910, he later had al-Shi'i executed.
He founded the coastal city of Mahdia; his invasions of Egypt failed.
RULER_RST_AL_QAIM_BIO:
Son of al-Mahdi, he reigned from 934 to 946.
His fleet raided the northern shores of the Mediterranean, sacking Genoa in 934–935.
The revolt of the Ibadi Abu Yazid, the man on the donkey, almost toppled him.
He died during the siege of Mahdia; his son al-Mansur crushed the revolt in 947.
RULER_RST_AL_MUIZZ_BIO:
He reigned from 953 to 975, one of the greatest Fatimid caliphs.
Around 958 his general Jawhar pushed west as far as the Atlantic.
In 969 Jawhar conquered Egypt and founded Cairo.
In 973 he moved to Cairo, leaving Ifriqiya and the Maghreb to the Zirid Buluggin.
RULER_RST_BULUGGIN_BIO:
Son of the Sanhaja Berber Ziri; by tradition he founded Algiers, Médéa and Miliana.
In 972–973 the Fatimid caliph, leaving for Cairo, made him governor of Ifriqiya.
In the west he fought the Zenata tribes and the allies of the Umayyads of Córdoba.
He died in 984; his son al-Mansur pursued a more independent course.
RULER_RST_BADIS_BIO:
Son of al-Mansur, Zirid emir from 996 to 1016.
He made his uncle Hammad lord of the western provinces, today's Algeria.
Around 1015 Hammad broke away and founded his own dynasty, ruling from the Qal'a of Beni Hammad.
Badis died in 1016 while besieging Hammad's fortress.
RULER_RST_AL_MUIZZ_ZIRI_BIO:
He became Zirid emir aged eight in 1016 and reigned until 1062.
In the 1040s he broke with the Shi'ite Fatimids and recognised the Abbasids of Baghdad.
In revenge the Fatimids unleashed the Arab nomads of the Banu Hilal on Ifriqiya.
Defeated at Haydaran in 1052, he fled from Kairouan to Mahdia in 1057.
RULER_RST_TAMIM_BIO:
Son of al-Mu'izz, he ruled from Mahdia from 1062 to 1108.
Because of the Hilali nomads, his state shrank to a narrow coastal strip.
In 1087 a Pisan and Genoese fleet sacked Mahdia and he had to pay a ransom.
He was also known as a poet; the Algerian coast was then held by the Hammadids of Béjaïa.
RULER_COR_HISHAM_I_BIO:
Son of Abd al-Rahman I, emir of Córdoba from 788 to 796.
A pious ruler, in whose time the Maliki school of law began to spread.
He put down his brothers' revolt and made war on the Christians of the north.
In 793 his armies reached Narbonne; the spoils helped pay for the mosque of Córdoba.
RULER_COR_AL_HAKAM_I_BIO:
Son of Hisham I, he reigned from 796 to 822.
By tradition he had the rebel notables of Toledo massacred in 797, the Day of the Ditch.
In 801 Louis the Pious took Barcelona from him.
In 818 he crushed the revolt of Córdoba's suburb; some of the exiles later seized Crete.
RULER_COR_ABD_AL_RAHMAN_II_BIO:
Son of al-Hakam I, he reigned 822–852 as Córdoba entered a cultural flowering.
He welcomed the Baghdad musician Ziryab, who set the fashions and tastes of the court.
In 844 the Vikings sacked Seville, but the emir's troops drove them off.
He exchanged embassies with Emperor Theophilos; the Martyrs of Córdoba began at the end of his reign.
RULER_COR_MUHAMMAD_I_BIO:
Son of Abd al-Rahman II, he reigned from 852 to 886.
In 859 he had Eulogius of Córdoba, leader of the Christian martyr movement, executed.
Toledo rebelled repeatedly, and around 880 Umar ibn Hafsun rose in revolt at Bobastro.
By tradition the Moorish fort from which Madrid later grew was built in his time.
RULER_COR_AL_MUNDHIR_BIO:
Son of Muhammad I, he reigned from 886 to 888.
Even as heir he had been his father's best general.
He marched against Ibn Hafsun and laid siege to Bobastro.
He died during the siege in 888; rumour said his brother Abdallah had poisoned him.
RULER_COR_ABDALLAH_BIO:
Son of Muhammad I, he reigned 888–912, the emirate's darkest years.
His power barely reached beyond Córdoba; rebel lords held the provinces.
In 891 he beat Ibn Hafsun at Poley; the rebel converted to Christianity around 899.
A suspicious man, he had several of his sons killed; his grandson Abd al-Rahman III succeeded him.
RULER_COR_ABD_AL_RAHMAN_III_BIO:
He reigned 912–961 and reunited al-Andalus; Bobastro finally fell in 928.
In 929 he proclaimed himself caliph, rivalling the Abbasids of Baghdad and the Fatimids.
He built the splendid palace city of Madinat al-Zahra; in 939 he was defeated at Simancas.
His Jewish physician and diplomat Hasdai ibn Shaprut reportedly wrote to the Khazar khagan.
RULER_COR_AL_HAKAM_II_BIO:
Son of Abd al-Rahman III, he reigned from 961 to 976.
A scholar-caliph, whose library was said to hold 400,000 volumes.
He enlarged the Great Mosque of Córdoba and adorned it with a magnificent mihrab.
He fought the Fatimids' allies in Morocco and drove off Viking raiders.
RULER_COR_HISHAM_II_BIO:
Son of al-Hakam II, he became caliph aged eleven in 976.
Real power lay with the hajib al-Mansur (Almanzor), the all-powerful chief minister.
Al-Mansur sacked Barcelona in 985 and Santiago de Compostela in 997.
Al-Mansur died in 1002; after his sons, Hisham was deposed in 1009 and civil war broke out.
RULER_COR_FITNA: the Fitna, the civil war of al-Andalus
RULER_COR_FITNA_BIO:
In 1009 a revolt overthrew the Amirid regime and Caliph Hisham II.
Rival claimants followed one another, backed by Berber mercenaries and Castilian and Catalan troops.
Between 1010 and 1013 the palace city of Madinat al-Zahra and Córdoba itself were sacked.
In 1031 the notables of Córdoba abolished the caliphate.
RULER_COR_TAIFAS_BIO:
After the caliphate fell, al-Andalus broke up into dozens of petty states, the taifas.
The lords of Seville, Toledo, Zaragoza, Granada and Badajoz also fought one another.
They paid tribute (parias) to the Christian kings; in 1085 Alfonso VI took Toledo.
They called in the Almoravids, who won at Sagrajas in 1086 and then swallowed the taifas.
RULER_AST_BERMUDO_I_BIO:
King of Asturias 789–791; a former deacon, hence his byname the Deacon.
Father of Ramiro I and ancestor of the later kings of Asturias and León.
In 791 he was defeated at Burbia by an army of the Emirate of Córdoba.
He then stepped down in favour of his kinsman Alfonso II and lived on in peace.
RULER_AST_ALFONSO_II: Alfonso II the Chaste, King of Asturias
RULER_AST_ALFONSO_II_BIO:
King of Asturias 791–842; his byname refers to his celibate, childless life.
He made Oviedo his capital and adorned it with churches and a palace.
In his reign the supposed tomb of the Apostle James was found at Compostela.
He kept in touch with Charlemagne and fought off repeated raids from Córdoba.
RULER_AST_RAMIRO_I_BIO:
King of Asturias 842–850, son of Bermudo I.
He first had to fight the usurper Nepotian for the throne.
In 844 he beat off a Viking raid on the Galician coast near A Coruña.
He built the fine halls on Monte Naranco; his victory at Clavijo is a later legend.
RULER_AST_ORDONO_I_BIO:
King of Asturias 850–866, son of Ramiro I.
He resettled León, Astorga, Tui and Amaya, pushing the frontier south.
In 859 he defeated Musa ibn Musa of the powerful Banu Qasi near Albelda.
During his reign Vikings also plundered the Galician coast.
RULER_AST_ALFONSO_III: Alfonso III the Great, King of Asturias
RULER_AST_ALFONSO_III_BIO:
King of Asturias 866–910; under him the kingdom reached its greatest extent.
His men took Porto in 868 and Coimbra in 878; the frontier ran along the Duero.
The Asturian chronicles written at his court stressed the Visigothic heritage.
In 910 his sons forced him from the throne; he died at Zamora that same year.
RULER_AST_GARCIA_I_BIO:
Eldest son of Alfonso III, who gained the throne in 910 by rebelling against his father.
He moved the royal seat from Oviedo to León and is counted as its first king.
His brothers Ordoño and Fruela governed Galicia and Asturias.
After a short reign he died at Zamora in 914, leaving no son.
RULER_AST_ORDONO_II_BIO:
King of León 914–924; before that he governed Galicia under his brother.
In 917 he won a victory over a Córdoban army at San Esteban de Gormaz.
In 920, however, Abd al-Rahman III crushed him at Valdejunquera.
He died in 924 and was briefly succeeded by his brother Fruela II.
RULER_AST_ALFONSO_IV: Alfonso IV the Monk, King of León
RULER_AST_ALFONSO_IV_BIO:
Son of Ordoño II; he took the throne of León in 925 after Fruela II died.
In 931 he abdicated in favour of his brother Ramiro and entered a monastery.
He soon regretted it and tried to win back the crown.
Ramiro captured and blinded him; he died around 933.
RULER_AST_RAMIRO_II_BIO:
King of León 931–951, one of the most successful Christian commanders of his age.
In 939 he defeated the great army of Caliph Abd al-Rahman III at Simancas.
After the victory he resettled the Tormes valley around Salamanca.
He struggled long with Count Fernán González of Castile, who sought autonomy.
RULER_AST_ORDONO_III_BIO:
Son of Ramiro II, King of León 951–956.
He had to defend his throne against his half-brother Sancho and Count Fernán González.
In 955 he led a successful raid as far as Lisbon.
He died young in 956 and was succeeded by his half-brother Sancho.
RULER_AST_SANCHO_I: Sancho I the Fat, King of León
RULER_AST_SANCHO_I_BIO:
King of León 956–958 and 960–966, son of Ramiro II.
Deposed in 958 because of his great obesity, he was replaced by Ordoño IV.
In Córdoba the physician Hasdai ibn Shaprut treated him; caliphal troops restored him.
He died in 966, by tradition poisoned by a Galician count.
RULER_AST_RAMIRO_III_BIO:
Son of Sancho I, he came to the throne in 966 at about five years old.
During his minority his aunt Elvira, a nun, ruled in his name.
His reign was shaken by revolts and by the devastating campaigns of Almanzor.
From 982 Bermudo rose against him as rival king; he died around 985.
RULER_AST_BERMUDO_II: Bermudo II the Gouty, King of León
RULER_AST_BERMUDO_II_BIO:
King of León 984–999; from 982 he had already been rival king in Galicia.
At first he relied on Almanzor's help, but later turned against him.
Almanzor sacked León and, in 997, Santiago de Compostela itself.
Captives carried Compostela's bells to Córdoba; Bermudo died in 999.
RULER_AST_ALFONSO_V: Alfonso V the Noble, King of León
RULER_AST_ALFONSO_V_BIO:
Son of Bermudo II, he became king in 999 at the age of five.
After Almanzor's death and the collapse of the Caliphate of Córdoba he rebuilt León.
Around 1017 he issued the Fuero of León, a key law code for city and kingdom.
He was killed by an arrow while besieging Viseu in 1028.
RULER_AST_BERMUDO_III_BIO:
Son of Alfonso V, King of León 1028–1037, last male of the old royal line.
He fought Sancho III of Navarre and Castile over the border lands.
His sister Sancha married Ferdinand of Castile.
In 1037 he fell at Tamarón fighting Ferdinand, and León passed to his brother-in-law.
RULER_AST_FERDINAND_I: Ferdinand I the Great, King of Castile and León
RULER_AST_FERDINAND_I_BIO:
Son of Sancho III of Navarre, lord of Castile, King of León by his wife's right from 1037.
In 1054 he defeated his brother García of Navarre at Atapuerca, where García fell.
He forced the Moorish taifa kingdoms to pay tribute and took Coimbra in 1064.
Before his death in 1065 he divided his realms among his sons.
RULER_AST_ALFONSO_VI: Alfonso VI of León and Castile
RULER_AST_ALFONSO_VI_BIO:
Son of Ferdinand I, King of León from 1065; his brother Sancho ousted him in 1072.
After Sancho's murder that year he united León, Castile and Galicia.
He took Toledo in 1085 but was defeated by the Almoravids at Sagrajas in 1086.
He styled himself emperor of all Spain, twice exiled El Cid, and died in 1109.
RULER_BEN_GRIMOALD_III_BIO:
Son of Arechis II, he had lived as a hostage at Charlemagne's court.
He was sent home in 787 on condition that he accept Frankish overlordship.
For a while he put Charles's name on his coins, then broke with the Franks.
He fended off the attacks of Pepin, King of Italy, and died childless in 806.
RULER_BEN_GRIMOALD_IV_BIO:
He had been his predecessor's treasurer, hence the byname Storesaiz.
He was elected prince in 806 after the death of Grimoald III.
In 812 he made peace with the Franks and agreed to pay them tribute.
Conspirators murdered him in 817; one of them, Sico, took his place.
RULER_BEN_SICO_BIO:
Gastald of Acerenza, he seized power after the murder of Grimoald IV.
Prince of Benevento 817–832.
He waged long wars against the Duchy of Naples and besieged the city.
In 831 he carried the relics of St Januarius from Naples to Benevento; he died in 832.
RULER_BEN_SICARD_BIO:
Son of Sico, Prince of Benevento 832–839.
He continued the war on Naples and also attacked Amalfi.
In 838 he brought the relics of the Apostle Bartholomew from Lipari to Benevento.
His cruelty made him many enemies, and he was assassinated in 839.
RULER_BEN_RADELCHIS_I_BIO:
Sicard's treasurer, he seized power in 839 after his lord's murder.
Sicard's brother Siconulf set himself up as rival prince in Salerno.
Both sides hired Saracen mercenaries in the civil war, who even took Bari.
In 849 Louis II split the realm into Benevento and Salerno; Radelchis died in 851.
RULER_BEN_ADELCHIS_BIO:
Son of Radelchis I, Prince of Benevento 854–878.
He fought beside Emperor Louis II against the Emirate of Bari, which fell in 871.
That same year he seized the emperor in Benevento and freed him only on oath.
He then sought Byzantine protection; his own kinsmen murdered him in 878.
RULER_BEN_AIO_BIO:
Son of Adelchis, Prince of Benevento 884–890, in troubled times.
His realm was threatened both by Saracen raids and by Byzantine expansion.
He fought the Byzantines for Apulia but gained no lasting success.
He died in 890; from 891 to 895 Byzantium occupied Benevento.
RULER_BEN_ATENULF_I: Atenulf I, Prince of Capua and Benevento
RULER_BEN_ATENULF_I_BIO:
Count of Capua who took Benevento in 900 and united the two principalities.
Capua–Benevento thus became the strongest Lombard state in southern Italy.
He sought an alliance with Byzantium and the pope against the Saracens on the Garigliano.
He died in 910; the Saracen base fell in 915 with the help of his son Landulf.
RULER_BEN_LANDULF_I: Landulf I, Prince of Capua and Benevento
RULER_BEN_LANDULF_I_BIO:
Son of Atenulf I, prince from 910, ruling jointly with his brother.
In 915 he joined the papal-Byzantine league that wiped out the Saracen base on the Garigliano.
Byzantium gave him high titles, yet he later invaded Byzantine Apulia.
He died in 943; his sons and grandsons ruled on until 961.
RULER_BEN_PANDULF_IRONHEAD: Pandulf Ironhead, Prince of Capua and Benevento
RULER_BEN_PANDULF_IRONHEAD_BIO:
Prince of Capua and Benevento 961–981 and a loyal ally of Emperor Otto I.
In 967 Otto also granted him the duchies of Spoleto and Camerino.
In 969 the Byzantines captured him at Bovino and took him to Constantinople.
In 978 he gained Salerno too, ruling most of southern Italy; he died in 981.
RULER_BEN_PANDULF_III_BIO:
Co-ruler with his father Landulf V, sole Prince of Benevento from 1033.
By now the principality had shrunk, and the Normans were growing strong around it.
Around 1050 the citizens expelled him and placed the city under the pope.
He returned in 1054 as a papal vassal and retired to a monastery in 1059.
RULER_BEN_PAPAL_BIO:
In 1051 Benevento submitted to Pope Leo IX, and Emperor Henry III gave up his rights.
After his defeat at Civitate in 1053, the pope was held by the Normans in Benevento.
The Lombard princes ruled as papal vassals until 1077, then the pope ruled directly.
The papal enclave, surrounded by Norman lands, survived until 1860.
POPE_ADRIAN_I_BIO:
Pope 772–795, from a Roman noble family.
He called on Charlemagne against the Lombard king Desiderius, who fell in 774.
His legates attended the Second Council of Nicaea (787), which restored icons.
His nearly 24-year reign was the longest for a millennium; Charlemagne gave him an epitaph.
POPE_LEO_III_BIO:
Pope 795–816; in 799 relatives of his predecessor attacked him in Rome.
He fled to Charlemagne at Paderborn, who restored him to office.
On Christmas Day 800 he crowned Charles emperor in St Peter's.
He refused to add the filioque to the Creed and had the text set up on silver shields.
POPE_STEPHEN_IV_BIO:
A Roman noble, pope from June 816 to January 817.
After his election he had the Romans swear loyalty to Emperor Louis the Pious.
In October 816 he anointed and crowned Louis and his wife at Reims.
He died only a few months after his return to Rome.
POPE_PASCHAL_I_BIO:
Pope 817–824; in 817 Louis the Pious confirmed the papal lands.
In 823 he crowned Louis's son Lothar emperor in Rome.
He built Santa Prassede and Santa Cecilia, famous for their mosaics.
Accused of the murder of two papal officials, he cleared himself by oath.
POPE_EUGENE_II_BIO:
Pope 824–827, candidate of the pro-Frankish Roman nobility.
In 824 he accepted the Constitutio Romana, which imposed strong imperial oversight.
Under it a pope-elect had to swear loyalty to the emperor before consecration.
His Roman synod of 826 ordered schools to be set up at bishops' seats.
POPE_GREGORY_IV_BIO:
Pope 827–844.
In 833 he tried to mediate between Louis the Pious and his rebel sons but was used by them.
He fortified Ostia against the Saracens, naming it Gregoriopolis.
He promoted the feast of All Saints on 1 November throughout the Church.
POPE_SERGIUS_II_BIO:
An elderly Roman aristocrat, pope 844–847.
He was consecrated without imperial approval, so Louis II marched on Rome with an army.
In 846 Saracen raiders plundered St Peter's, then outside the city walls.
His reign was marred by the simony and greed of his brother Benedict.
POPE_LEO_IV_BIO:
Pope 847–855, elected after the Saracen raid of 846.
He walled in the Vatican; the district became known as the Leonine City.
In 849 a united Italian fleet smashed a Saracen fleet off Ostia.
In 853 he received the young Alfred, later Alfred the Great, in Rome.
POPE_BENEDICT_III_BIO:
Pope 855–858.
Imperial envoys briefly installed Anastasius, later the Librarian, as antipope.
The Roman clergy and people stood by Benedict, and he regained office within days.
The late medieval legend of Pope Joan placed the female pope just before him.
POPE_NICHOLAS_I_BIO:
Pope 858–867, known as the Great, one of the strongest early medieval popes.
In 863 he deposed Patriarch Photius of Constantinople, causing a grave schism.
He refused to let King Lothar II divorce his wife Theutberga.
In 866 he answered the newly converting Bulgarians in a long letter of instruction.
POPE_ADRIAN_II_BIO:
Pope 867–872; he had been married before his ordination.
In 868 a Roman noble abducted and killed his wife and daughter.
He approved the Slavonic liturgy of Cyril and Methodius and made Methodius a bishop.
His legates attended the Council of Constantinople of 869–870, which condemned Photius.
POPE_JOHN_VIII_BIO:
Pope 872–882; he crowned Charles the Bald emperor in 875 and Charles the Fat in 881.
He organised war against the Saracens but in the end had to pay them tribute.
In 880 he again allowed Methodius's Slavonic liturgy.
In 882 he was poisoned and then clubbed to death, the first pope to be murdered.
POPE_MARINUS_I_BIO:
Pope 882–884; a seasoned diplomat who had been legate to Constantinople several times.
He was the first pope who was already bishop of another see when elected.
He lifted the sentence against the exiled Formosus and recalled him.
He died in 884; after Adrian III's brief reign Stephen V followed.
POPE_STEPHEN_V_BIO:
Pope 885–891; Rome was suffering famine when he took office.
He banned the Slavonic liturgy, and Methodius's disciples were driven out of Moravia.
The fleeing disciples carried on their work in Bulgaria.
In 891 he crowned Guy of Spoleto emperor and died later that year.
POPE_FORMOSUS_BIO:
Pope 891–896; earlier Bishop of Porto and a missionary to the Bulgarians.
He crowned Lambert of Spoleto emperor in 892 and the East Frankish Arnulf in 896.
In 897 his successor had his corpse exhumed and put on trial in the Cadaver Synod.
896–904 saw many short, chaotic pontificates, including the Magyar raid of 899.
POPE_SERGIUS_III_BIO:
Pope 904–911, a bitter enemy of Formosus.
He declared Formosus's ordinations invalid and upheld the Cadaver Synod.
He relied on the family of Theophylact; Liutprand calls him Marozia's lover.
He rebuilt the Lateran basilica; two short pontificates followed until 914.
POPE_JOHN_X_BIO:
Archbishop of Ravenna, pope 914–928.
In 915 he personally led the allied army against the Saracens on the Garigliano.
The same year he crowned Berengar I emperor.
He clashed with Marozia, who imprisoned him; he died in prison in 928, probably smothered.
POPE_JOHN_XI_BIO:
Son of Marozia, made pope in 931 at about twenty through his mother's power.
Liutprand claims his father was Pope Sergius III, though this is disputed.
In 932 his half-brother Alberic II rebelled and took control of Rome and the pope.
He granted privileges to the abbey of Cluny; he died in late 935 or early 936.
POPE_LEO_VII_BIO:
Pope 936–939, chosen by Alberic II, lord of Rome.
He backed the monastic reforms of Abbot Odo of Cluny in and around Rome.
He helped broker peace between Alberic and King Hugh of Italy.
Stephen VIII and Marinus II followed until 946, both in Alberic's shadow.
POPE_AGAPETUS_II_BIO:
Pope 946–955, while Alberic II ruled Rome.
Under Alberic's pressure he refused Otto I's request to be crowned emperor in Rome.
He supported church reform and the German church's missions to the north.
Alberic made the Romans swear to elect his son Octavian pope after Agapetus.
POPE_JOHN_XII_BIO:
Octavian, son of Alberic II, became lord of Rome and pope in 955 at about 18.
In 962 he crowned Otto I emperor and approved plans for an archbishopric at Magdeburg.
He then plotted against Otto, whose synod deposed him in 963.
Notorious for his scandalous life, he died in 964; rival popes followed until 965.
POPE_JOHN_XIII_BIO:
Pope 965–972, the candidate of Emperor Otto I.
The Romans drove him out in 965, but Otto's army restored him in 966.
He crowned Otto II co-emperor in 967 and married him to Theophanu in 972.
In 968 he created the Archbishopric of Magdeburg; his successor Benedict VI was killed in 974.
POPE_BENEDICT_VII_BIO:
Pope 974–983, backed by Emperor Otto II.
He drove out the antipope Boniface VII, who had seized power through murder.
In 981 a synod under him condemned simony; he supported monastic reform.
Under John XIV and the returning Boniface, chaos reigned again until 985.
POPE_JOHN_XV_BIO:
Pope 985–996, under the influence of the Crescentii family.
In 993 he canonised Bishop Ulrich of Augsburg, the first known papal canonisation.
In 991 he mediated between Æthelred of England and the Duke of Normandy.
He died in 996; his successor Gregory V (996–999) was the first German pope.
POPE_SYLVESTER_II_BIO:
Gerbert of Aurillac, the greatest scholar of his day, pope 999–1003, the first French pope.
He promoted the abacus and Arabic numerals and was tutor and ally of Otto III.
By tradition he sent a crown to Stephen I of Hungary around 1000.
The Archbishopric of Gniezno was founded in 1000; he died in 1003.
POPE_BENEDICT_VIII_BIO:
Of the Counts of Tusculum, pope 1012–1024; three short pontificates preceded him from 1003.
In 1014 he crowned Henry II emperor; the Creed was then first sung in Rome with the filioque.
In 1016 his fleet drove the Saracens out of the Luni region.
At the Synod of Pavia in 1022 he demanded clerical celibacy; he died in 1024.
POPE_JOHN_XIX_BIO:
Brother of Benedict VIII, pope 1024–1032.
A layman, he received all holy orders in a single day.
In 1027 he crowned Conrad II emperor, with King Cnut in attendance.
For Byzantine gold he was ready to grant Constantinople's patriarch an ecumenical title, but drew back.
POPE_BENEDICT_IX_BIO:
A scion of the Tusculum family, he became pope very young in 1032.
He held the papacy three times: 1032–1044, in 1045 and 1047–1048.
In 1045 he sold the office to his godfather, Gregory VI.
Henry III restored order at Sutri in 1046; German popes followed until 1049.
POPE_LEO_IX_BIO:
Bruno of Egisheim, Bishop of Toul, pope 1049–1054 and a great figure of church reform.
In 1052 he mediated between Henry III and Andrew I of Hungary at the siege of Pressburg.
In 1053 the Normans defeated him at Civitate and held him in Benevento.
After his death his legates excommunicated Patriarch Cerularius in 1054, the Great Schism.
POPE_NICHOLAS_II_BIO:
Gerard of Burgundy, pope 1058/1059–1061, after Victor II and Stephen IX.
His decree of 1059 placed papal elections in the hands of the cardinals.
That year at Melfi he made Robert Guiscard Duke of Apulia, Calabria and Sicily.
The Normans thus became papal vassals and military allies; he died in 1061.
POPE_ALEXANDER_II_BIO:
Anselm of Baggio, Bishop of Lucca, pope 1061–1073.
The German court set up the antipope Cadalus (Honorius II) against him.
In 1064 he promised remission of sins to those fighting at Barbastro in Spain.
Norman sources say he sent a banner to William the Conqueror for the invasion of 1066.
POPE_GREGORY_VII_BIO:
Hildebrand, leader of the reform papacy, pope 1073–1085.
His Dictatus papae of 1075 asserted universal papal power; the Investiture Contest began.
Henry IV came to him as a penitent at Canossa in 1077; he also claimed Hungary as St Peter's fief.
After Robert Guiscard sacked Rome in 1084, he died in exile at Salerno.
POPE_URBAN_II_BIO:
Odo of Châtillon, a monk of Cluny, pope 1088–1099; Victor III preceded him.
At Piacenza in 1095 he received envoys of Emperor Alexios asking for help.
Later that year at Clermont he proclaimed the First Crusade.
He died in July 1099, two weeks after Jerusalem fell, before the news reached him.
POPE_PASCHAL_II_BIO:
Rainerius, a monk, pope 1099–1118, successor of Urban II.
He carried on the Investiture Contest with the German rulers.
In 1111 Henry V took him captive and forced concessions that he later revoked.
In 1107 he reached a compromise with Henry I of England.
RULER_ESL_TRIBES_BIO:
Ilmen Slovenes, Krivichs, Polans, Severians, Drevlians and Vyatichi lived under their own princes.
They dwelt in hillforts amid forests and rivers, worshipping Perun and other old gods.
By the chronicle, the southern tribes paid tribute to the Khazars, the northern ones to the Varangians.
Their rivers carried furs, honey and slaves toward Byzantium and the caliphate.
RULER_ESL_ASKOLD_DIR_BIO:
According to the Primary Chronicle, they left Rurik's Varangian retinue and became lords of Kiev.
Tradition credits them with the Rus attack on Constantinople in 860.
Byzantine sources report that some of the Rus accepted baptism soon afterwards.
In 882 Oleg lured them out of the city by a ruse and had both killed.
RULER_ESL_TRIBAL_PRINCES: The tribal princes tributary to Kiev
RULER_ESL_TRIBAL_PRINCES_BIO:
After 882 Oleg forced the Drevlians, Severians and Radimichs one by one to pay tribute to Kiev.
The tribes kept their own princes but paid the Kievan prince in furs and silver.
On the winter round called poliudie, the prince and his retinue toured their lands to collect it.
By the chronicle, their warriors joined the Rus campaign against Byzantium in 907.
RULER_ESL_MAL_BIO:
In 945 the Drevlians killed Prince Igor of Kiev when he came back to collect tribute a second time.
Mal then sent envoys to ask for the hand of Igor's widow, Olga.
By the chronicle, Olga had the envoys buried alive and burned, and turned the funeral feast into a massacre.
In 946 she burned Iskorosten using its own pigeons and sparrows; Mal's fate is unknown.
RULER_ESL_UNDER_RUS_BIO:
After Olga's reforms, tribal lands were run by Kievan governors and tribute stations called pogosts.
