Around 964 Sviatoslav made even the Vyatichi pay tribute to Kiev instead of the Khazars.
Vladimir set his sons over the tribal centres and spread Christianity after 988.
Tribal names slowly faded from the chronicle, though the Vyatichi long stayed pagan.
RULER_ESL_KHODOTA_BIO:
In the Oka forests the Vyatichi kept their independence and pagan faith until the late 11th century.
Khodota and his son are known only from Vladimir Monomakh's Instruction.
Monomakh led two winter campaigns against him into Vyatichi land, probably in the 1080s.
By tradition, the monk Kuksha was still martyred among them in the early 12th century.
RULER_BAL_ELDERS_BIO:
Along the eastern Baltic shore, the tribes were led by elders, chieftains and wealthy landholders.
They had no common king; assemblies of villages and hillforts decided on war and peace.
Wulfstan, a late 9th-century traveller, wrote that the land of the Este had many forts, each with a king.
They sold amber, furs and wax, and alternately traded and fought with the Scandinavians.
RULER_BAL_CURONIANS: The Curonian kings who defied the Swedes
RULER_BAL_CURONIANS_BIO:
Once tributary to the Swedes, the Curonians rebelled in the 850s and refused to pay.
According to Rimbert's Life of Ansgar, they also routed and plundered a Danish raiding fleet.
King Olof of the Swedes then took Seeburg (Grobiņa) and besieged Apulia (Apuolė).
After eight days the Curonians gave ransom and hostages and promised tribute again.
RULER_BAL_PRUSSIANS_BIO:
In 997 Saint Adalbert of Prague, who by tradition baptized Stephen of Hungary, went to the Prussians.
He came with Bolesław the Brave's backing, but the Prussians saw him as an enemy of their gods and ways.
On 23 April 997 a band led by a pagan priest killed him; Bolesław ransomed his body for gold.
The chiefs went on resisting conversion and conquest for two more centuries.
RULER_KHZ_KAGANS: The sacral khagan and the bek
RULER_KHZ_KAGANS_BIO:
The Khazar khagan was a sacred figure, rarely seen by his subjects and reigning only symbolically.
Real power lay with the bek, who led the army and ran the affairs of the realm.
Their seat was Itil in the Volga delta, where Muslim, Jewish, Christian and pagan judges sat.
The empire lived on tolls and tribute, and the Magyars long belonged to its circle of allies.
RULER_KHZ_OBADIAH_BIO:
According to King Joseph's letter, Obadiah descended from Bulan, the first Khazar ruler to adopt Judaism.
He renewed the kingdom and made rabbinic Judaism the faith of its ruling circle.
He built synagogues and houses of study and invited Jewish sages to the land.
Scholars date him to around 800, but he is known only from this tradition.
RULER_KHZ_BENJAMIN_BIO:
He appears in the king list of Joseph's letter and is dated to the late 9th century.
According to the Schechter Letter, several neighbouring peoples allied against Khazaria in his day.
The king of the Alans fought on the Khazar side and helped drive the attackers back.
Pecheneg pressure was also growing, and it would eventually push the Magyars west.
RULER_KHZ_AARON_II_BIO:
By Joseph's letter he was Benjamin's son, ruling in the early decades of the 10th century.
According to the Schechter Letter, the Byzantines incited the Alans against him.
Aaron defeated them with hired Oghuz troops and captured the Alan king.
He sealed the peace by marrying his son Joseph to the Alan king's daughter.
RULER_KHZ_JOSEPH_BIO:
Son of Aaron II, he ruled in the mid-10th century and is the best-known Khazar ruler.
He answered a letter from Hasdai ibn Shaprut, the Jewish courtier of the caliph of Córdoba.
His reply described his realm, its peoples and how the Khazar kings came to Judaism.
In his day the Khazars could still repel the Rus, but the empire was already in decline.
RULER_KHZ_REMNANT: The lords of the Khazar remnant
RULER_KHZ_REMNANT_BIO:
Around 965 Prince Sviatoslav of Kiev took Sarkel and then sacked Itil.
The Khazar empire collapsed; some refugees fled to islands in the Caspian Sea.
Some Arab sources say they won Khwarazm's help only by converting to Islam.
Small Khazar lordships lived on for a time in Crimea and the North Caucasus foothills.
RULER_KHZ_GEORGIUS_TZUL_BIO:
Skylitzes calls him ruler of Khazaria; his lands probably lay in and around Crimea.
In 1016 Basil II sent a fleet against him under the commander Mongus.
The Byzantines were aided by Sphengus, whom Skylitzes calls a brother of Vladimir of Kiev.
He was captured in the first clash, the last Khazar ruler named in the sources.
RULER_VBU_CHIEFS_BIO:
After the fall of Great Bulgaria, Bulgar clans moved north to where the Volga meets the Kama.
Their chiefs lived under the overlordship of the Khazar khagan and paid him tribute.
Their land linked the northern fur routes with the river trade toward the Caspian.
Mixing with local Finno-Ugric and Turkic peoples, they slowly grew into one people.
RULER_VBU_ALMISH: Almış, king of the Volga Bulgars
RULER_VBU_ALMISH_BIO:
Son of Shilki, he bore the title yiltawar and ruled the Volga Bulgars as a Khazar vassal.
Seeking to break free of the Khazars, he asked Caliph al-Muqtadir for help and craftsmen.
In 922 Ibn Fadlan's embassy reached him; its travel account is our main source on him.
He embraced Islam, took the name Jafar ibn Abdallah and had the Friday sermon read for the caliph.
RULER_VBU_MIKAIL_BIO:
Son of Almış, he succeeded his father as emir of the Volga Bulgars.
His name survives on locally struck silver dirhams; the sources say little else about him.
Under him Islam spread further and trade with the Samanid lands flourished.
By now Khazar overlordship was becoming more and more nominal.
RULER_VBU_ABDALLAH_BIO:
Son of Mikail; his name survives on dirhams struck in the 940s.
In his time the towns of Bulgar and Suvar grew into thriving trade centres.
Arab geographers say the Bulgars sold furs, wax and slaves to merchants from the south.
Rus merchant boats were regular visitors at the Volga markets.
RULER_VBU_TALIB_BIO:
His name survives on silver coins struck in the 970s; little else is known of him.
By his time the Khazar empire lay in ruins and the Volga Bulgars were masters of the middle Volga.
Around 985 Prince Vladimir of Kiev campaigned against the Bulgars and then made peace with them.
By the chronicle, Muslim Bulgar envoys also came to Kiev to win Vladimir for their faith.
RULER_VBU_TRADE_EMIRS_BIO:
According to the late historian Tatishchev, the Volga Bulgars made a trade treaty with Kiev in 1006.
Their merchants, carrying sealed permits, could travel the rivers and trade in the Rus towns.
By the chronicle, Bulgar grain saved the people of Suzdal during the famine of 1024.
Raids broke the peace, however: in 1088 the Volga Bulgars captured Murom.
RULER_AGH_GOVERNORS_BIO:
From Kairouan they ruled Ifriqiya, roughly today's Tunisia, in the name of the caliph in Baghdad.
They fought constantly with Kharijite Berbers and the unruly Arab garrison, the jund.
Harthama ibn Ayan built the ribat of Monastir in 796, one of the first forts on the coast.
When the army rose against his successor, Ibrahim ibn al-Aghlab, governor of the Zab, restored order.
RULER_AGH_IBRAHIM_I_BIO:
In 800 Caliph Harun al-Rashid made him hereditary emir of Ifriqiya.
In return he promised a yearly tribute of 40,000 dinars and gave up the subsidy from Egypt.
He built a new residence, al-Abbasiyya, near Kairouan and formed a guard of slave soldiers.
He crushed the garrison's revolts and had secured his dynasty by his death in 812.
RULER_AGH_ABDALLAH_I_BIO:
Son of Ibrahim I, he ruled Ifriqiya from 812 to 817.
He replaced the harvest tithe with a fixed money tax, which caused widespread anger.
The chronicles remember him as a greedy and harsh ruler.
He died in 817 and was succeeded by his brother Ziyadat Allah.
RULER_AGH_ZIYADAT_ALLAH_I_BIO:
He ruled from 817 to 838, one of the strongest and most embattled emirs of the dynasty.
From 824 a revolt of the jund under Mansur al-Tunbudhi nearly overthrew him.
In 827 he sent a fleet to Sicily under the qadi Asad ibn al-Furat; it landed at Mazara.
Palermo fell in 831; in Kairouan he rebuilt the Great Mosque.
RULER_AGH_AL_AGHLAB_BIO:
Brother of Ziyadat Allah I, he ruled from 838 to 841.
He placated the jund by settling the soldiers' pay and dismissing hated officials.
According to the sources, he banned the sale of wine in Kairouan.
In his time the conquest of Sicily advanced and more fortresses fell to the Muslims.
RULER_AGH_MUHAMMAD_I_BIO:
Son of al-Aghlab, he ruled from 841 to 856; the sources say he enjoyed power more than he wielded it.
One of his brothers rose against him, but he managed to regain control.
In 848 he made the revered Sahnun qadi of Kairouan, who entrenched the Maliki school of law.
The conquest of Sicily went on, and Messina fell around 842–843.
RULER_AGH_AHMAD_BIO:
He ruled from 856 to 863; the sources remember him as a kindly and generous emir.
He enlarged the Great Mosque of Kairouan, whose mihrab was faced with lustre tiles from Baghdad.
The great reservoirs of Kairouan, the so-called Aghlabid basins, were built in his reign.
In 859 his troops took Enna in Sicily, one of the chief Byzantine strongholds.
RULER_AGH_ZIYADAT_ALLAH_II_BIO:
Brother of Ahmad, he came to the throne on his brother's death in 863.
He reigned for barely a year and died in 864.
The sources record almost nothing of his short rule.
He was succeeded by his nephew Muhammad II, Ahmad's son.
RULER_AGH_MUHAMMAD_II_BIO:
Son of Ahmad, he ruled from 864 to 875; his nickname, Abu'l-Gharaniq, refers to his love of crane hunting.
The sources paint him as a pleasure-seeker devoted to hunting and feasting.
In his reign, in 870, the Muslims captured Malta.
He died young in 875 and was succeeded by his brother Ibrahim II.
RULER_AGH_IBRAHIM_II_BIO:
He ruled from 875 to 902 and built a new residence, Raqqada, near Kairouan.
In 878 his troops took Syracuse after a nine-month siege.
His cruelty was notorious: he executed rebels and even his own relatives in large numbers.
He abdicated in 902, took Taormina in Sicily and died besieging Cosenza in Calabria.
RULER_AGH_ABDALLAH_II_BIO:
Son of Ibrahim II, he took over the rule of Ifriqiya when his father abdicated in 902.
He was considered capable and tried to soften his father's harsh regime.
By then the Shiite movement among the Kutama Berbers had become a serious threat.
In 903 he was murdered by his own servants, by tradition at the urging of his son Ziyadat Allah.
RULER_AGH_ZIYADAT_ALLAH_III: Ziyadat Allah III, the last Aghlabid
RULER_AGH_ZIYADAT_ALLAH_III_BIO:
He took the throne in 903 after his father's murder and had his brothers and uncles executed.
Amid his court's pleasures he failed to stop the Kutama Berbers of Abu Abdallah al-Shii.
In March 909 his army was routed at al-Urbus, and he fled to Egypt with his treasure.
He sought help from Baghdad in vain and died in Palestine around 916, while the Fatimids ruled Ifriqiya.

UNIT_GESITH_DESC: The king's companions: armoured, heavily armed foot. Best in the shield wall, they break levies, but volleys of arrows wear them down.
UNIT_BERSERKER_DESC: Warriors born for the charge: terrifying in attack, they sweep away levies and archers, but a wall of spears or shields breaks them, and they are poor defenders.
UNIT_SCARA_DESC: The iron-clad horsemen (scara) of the Frankish kings and Norman dukes. On open ground their charge decides the battle and scatters archers and levies – but against spears, in hills, forest and marsh they lose much of their strength.
UNIT_LONGBOW_DESC: Bowmen of the Welsh and Breton valleys: their volleys thin out infantry, and they are even stronger in the hills. Against a cavalry charge they are defenceless.
UNIT_KERN_DESC: Gaelic light infantry: quick and dangerous in forest, marsh and hills, they overrun archers; weak against heavy cavalry and armoured foot.
UNIT_SPEARMEN_DESC: The Saxon spear wall: the best answer to cavalry – a charge breaks on it.
UNIT_FOREST_ARCHER_DESC: Archers of the Slavic forests: they shoot from among the trees and thin out infantry; best in forest, weak against cavalry.
UNIT_HUNTER_DESC: Hunters of the Baltic and Finnish woods: they fight with the bow and are best in forest and marsh.
UNIT_SKI_HUNTER_DESC: Hunters of the Sámi and the far north: swift and hardy, they strike from ambush in forest and hills.
UNIT_HORSE_ARCHER_DESC: The weapon of the steppe peoples: on open ground they shoot infantry from afar and ride off before they can be reached. Weaker in forest, hills and marsh, and hunted by light cavalry.
UNIT_CATAPHRACT_DESC: The mailed cavalry of the Byzantine and Georgian armies, horse and rider in armour: the strongest charge, but costly, and it loses strength against spears and on rough ground.
UNIT_LIGHT_CAV_DESC: The swift horsemen of the Arab armies: they ride down archers and horse archers, but are weak against spears and the shield wall.
UNIT_MILITIA_DESC: Spear-armed townsmen and hillmen of the Latin lands: cheap, and they hold well against cavalry.
